<!-- mainthm-1: body_md -->
\label{thmA}
Let $n\ge2$ and $h\in(\mathbb{F}_q^\times)^n$. Then $H^i_c\big(Y_h\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(\sum_iu_i^{-1})\big)=0$ for $i\ne n-1$, and $H^{n-1}_c$ has dimension $2^n-1$. Its Frobenius eigenvalues are $r(n)$ eigenvalues of weight $n-1$ together with, for each $1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, the eigenvalue $q^{k-1}$ with multiplicity $m_{n,k}$. Consequently
\[
\Sigma_n(h)=(-1)^{n-1}\Big(\tau_q(h)+\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}m_{n,k}\,q^{k-1}\Big),\qquad|\tau_q(h)|\le r(n)\,q^{(n-1)/2},
\]
where $\tau_q(h)$ is the sum of the eigenvalues of weight $n-1$.
<!-- end mainthm-1 -->
<!-- mainthm-2: body_md -->
\label{thmB}
Let $S=\mathbb{G}_m^n$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$, with coordinates $h=(h_1,\dots,h_n)$. There is a lisse sheaf $\mathcal G_n$ of rank $2^n-1$ on $S$ whose stalk at a geometric point $h$ is $H^{n-1}_c\big(Y_h,\mathcal{L}_\psi(\sum_iu_i^{-1})\big)(-1)$. It carries a filtration by lisse subsheaves whose graded pieces are the geometrically constant sheaves $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell(-k)^{\oplus m_{n,k}}$ for $1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, and a lisse sheaf $\mathcal W_n$, pure of weight $n+1$ and of rank $r(n)$, as top quotient. For $h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)$,
\[
\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_h\mid\mathcal W_n)=(-1)^{n-1}q\,\Sigma_n(h)-\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}m_{n,k}\,q^k .
\]
<!-- end mainthm-2 -->
<!-- mainthm-3: body_md -->
\label{thmC}
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}$ is tamely ramified at $h_1=0$, and its local monodromy there is unipotent, with $r(n-1)$ Jordan blocks of size $2$, $\kappa_1$ blocks of size $1$, and no block of size $\ge3$.
\item The local monodromy of $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}$ at $h_1=\infty$ is the direct sum of a tame part and a part of dimension $2^{n-1}$ that is isoclinic of slope $1$. The tame part is unipotent, with $\kappa_j$ Jordan blocks of size $j-2$ for every $j\ge3$. The part of slope $1$ is of the form $\mathcal{L}_\psi(-h_1/\lambda)\otimes X$, where all slopes of $X$ are $<1$. In particular $\operatorname{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})=2^{n-1}$.
\item $\det(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})$ is geometrically isomorphic to $\mathcal{L}_\psi(-2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}h_1)$.
\item The perverse sheaf $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}[1]$ is isomorphic to the multiplicative middle convolution of $\mathrm{Kl}[1]$ with $\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1]$, where $\iota(t)=t^{-1}$ and $\mathcal M_c=\bigotimes_{i=2}^n[\times c_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end mainthm-3 -->
<!-- mainthm-4: body_md -->
\label{thmD}
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For every $n\ge2$ and every $q$,
\[
\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}\Sigma_n(h)=(-1)^nq^{n-1},\qquad\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}|\Sigma_n(h)|^2=q^{n-2}\Big((q-1)^{n+1}+1-(-1)^n(q-2)\Big).
\]
\item For every $n\ge3$,
\[
\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}|\Sigma_n(h)|^4=2q^{3n-2}+O_n\big(q^{3n-2-\delta(n)}\big),\qquad\delta(n)=\min\Big(1,\frac{n-2}2\Big).
\]
\item For $n=2$ and fixed $p$, $\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^2}|\Sigma_2(h)|^4=2q^4+O_p\big(q^{7/2}\big)$ as $q\to\infty$ through powers of $p$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end mainthm-4 -->
<!-- mainthm-5: body_md -->
\label{thmE}
Let $n\ge2$ and let $p$ be an odd prime.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $\det\mathcal W_n\cong\mathcal{L}_\psi(-2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}(h_1+\cdots+h_n))\otimes\alpha^{\deg}$ with $\alpha=p^{(n+1)r(n)/2}$, where $\alpha^{\deg}$ is the geometrically constant sheaf on which $\operatorname{Frob}_p$ acts by $\alpha$. Equivalently, by Theorem~\ref{thmB} and the Chebotarev density theorem, for every power $q$ of $p$ and every $h\in(\mathbb{F}_q^\times)^n$, the product of the $r(n)$ eigenvalues of weight $n-1$ in Theorem~\ref{thmA} is $q^{(n-1)r(n)/2}\psi_q\big(-2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}(h_1+\cdots+h_n)\big)$, and
\[
\det\Big(\operatorname{Frob}_q\mid H^{n-1}_c\big(Y_h\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(\textstyle\sum_iu_i^{-1})\big)\Big)=q^{(n-2)2^{n-1}+1}\,\psi_q\big(-2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}(h_1+\cdots+h_n)\big).
\]
\item The geometric monodromy group of $\mathcal W_n$ is
\[
G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)=\big\{g\in\operatorname{GL}_{r(n)}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell):\det(g)^p=1\big\}.
\]
In particular $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)^0=\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}$, and the component group is cyclic of order $p$.
\item Let $\mathcal W_n^0=\mathcal W_n\otimes\gamma^{\deg}$, where $\gamma\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$ corresponds to the positive real number $p^{-(n+1)/2}$. Then $\mathcal W_n^0$ is pure of weight $0$, and its arithmetic monodromy group is equal to $G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end mainthm-5 -->
<!-- mainthm-6: body_md -->
\label{thmF}
Let $n\ge2$, let $p$ be an odd prime, and let $K_n=\{g\in\mathrm U(r(n)):\det(g)^p=1\}$. As $q\to\infty$ through powers of $p$, the $(q-1)^n$ complex numbers
\[
q^{-(n-1)/2}\big((-1)^{n-1}\Sigma_n(h)-c_n(q)\big),\qquad h\in(\mathbb{F}_q^\times)^n,
\]
become equidistributed with respect to the image under $g\mapsto\operatorname{Tr} g$ of the Haar probability measure on $K_n$. In particular, the numbers $q^{-(n-1)/2}\big|\Sigma_n(h)-(-1)^{n-1}c_n(q)\big|$ become equidistributed with respect to the law of $|\operatorname{Tr} g|$ for $g$ a Haar-random element of $\mathrm{SU}(r(n))$.
<!-- end mainthm-6 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:factor}
For every $h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n$ the identity \eqref{eq:intro-factor} holds. If exactly $a$ coordinates of $h$ are nonzero and $h'\in(\mathbb{F}_q^\times)^a$ is the vector they form, then $\Sigma_n(h)=0$ if $a=0$, $|\Sigma_n(h)|=1$ if $a=1$, and $\Sigma_n(h)=(-1)^{n-a}\Sigma_a(h')$ if $a\ge2$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Insert $\mathbf 1_{\langle h,u\rangle=-\lambda}=q^{-1}\sum_{t\in\mathbb{F}_q}\psi_q\big(t(\lambda+\langle h,u\rangle)\big)$ into \eqref{eq:intro-Sigma}. The sum over $u$ factors, and the factor indexed by $i$ is $\sum_{u_i\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times}\psi_q(u_i^{-1}+th_iu_i)=K(th_i)$. If $h_i=0$, the variable $u_i$ does not occur in the constraint, and summing over it contributes the factor $\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times}\psi_q(x^{-1})=-1$. If $a=0$ the constraint reads $0=-\lambda$, which is impossible. If $a=1$ it determines the remaining variable, and the sum has a single term.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:integrate-t}
Let $V$ be a scheme of finite type over a field of characteristic $p$, $g\colon V\to\mathbb A^1$ a morphism, $i\colon Y=g^{-1}(0)\hookrightarrow V$ the inclusion, and $q_V\colon V\times\mathbb A^1_t\to V$ the projection. Then $Rq_{V!}\mathcal{L}_\psi(tg)\cong i_*\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell(-1)[-2]$. Hence, for every constructible complex $K$ on $V$,
\[
Rq_{V!}\big(q_V^*K\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(tg)\big)\cong i_*(K|_Y)(-1)[-2],
\]
and the formation of these isomorphisms commutes with base change $V'\to V$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $p_s\colon\mathbb A^1_s\times\mathbb A^1_t\to\mathbb A^1_s$ be the projection. For a geometric point $s\ne0$, the sheaf $\mathcal{L}_\psi(st)$ on $\mathbb A^1_t$ is lisse of rank one and geometrically nontrivial, with Swan conductor $1$ at $\infty$. The Grothendieck--Ogg--Shafarevich formula gives Euler characteristic $1-1=0$; as $H^0_c$ and $H^2_c$ vanish, all its compactly supported cohomology vanishes. For $s=0$ one obtains $H^*_c(\mathbb A^1,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell)=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell(-1)[-2]$. By proper base change for $Rp_{s!}$, the stalk of $Rp_{s!}\mathcal{L}_\psi(st)$ at a geometric point $s$ is $R\Gamma_c(\mathbb A^1_t\otimes k(s),\mathcal{L}_\psi(st))$. So the cohomology sheaves of $Rp_{s!}\mathcal{L}_\psi(st)$ are supported at $s=0$, with stalk $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell(-1)$ in degree $2$, and $Rp_{s!}\mathcal{L}_\psi(st)\cong i_{0*}\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell(-1)[-2]$. Since $\mathcal{L}_\psi(tg)=(g\times\mathrm{id})^*\mathcal{L}_\psi(st)$, proper base change along $g$ gives the first isomorphism, and the projection formula gives the second.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:breaks}
Let $x$ be a closed point of a smooth curve over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$, and let $V,V'$ be finite-dimensional continuous representations of $I_x$.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item Every break of $V\otimes V'$ is at most the largest of the breaks of $V$ and $V'$.
\item If all breaks of $V$ are $<s'$ and $V'$ is isoclinic of break $s'>0$, then $V\otimes V'$ is isoclinic of break $s'$. In particular $\operatorname{Swan}_x(V\otimes V')=s'\dim V\dim V'$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $(I^{(r)})_{r\ge0}$ be the upper numbering filtration of $I_x$, and let $I^{(r+)}$ be the closure of $\bigcup_{r'>r}I^{(r')}$. A representation $W$ has all breaks $\le r$ if and only if $I^{(r+)}$ acts trivially on $W$, and it is isoclinic of break $s>0$ if and only if $I^{(s+)}$ acts trivially on $W$ and $W^{I^{(r+)}}=0$ for $0\le r<s$ \cite[1.1]{Katz-Gauss}. Statement~(i) is clear, because $I^{(r+)}$ acts trivially on $V\otimes V'$ as soon as it acts trivially on both factors. For (ii), let $s<s'$ be the largest break of $V$. By (i), $I^{(s'+)}$ acts trivially on $V\otimes V'$. If $s\le r<s'$, then $I^{(r+)}$ acts trivially on $V$, so $(V\otimes V')^{I^{(r+)}}=V\otimes V'^{I^{(r+)}}=0$. If $0\le r<s$, then $I^{(r+)}\supseteq I^{(s+)}$, and therefore $(V\otimes V')^{I^{(r+)}}\subseteq(V\otimes V')^{I^{(s+)}}=0$ by the previous case. Hence $V\otimes V'$ is isoclinic of break $s'$, and its Swan conductor is $s'\dim(V\otimes V')$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:CG}
Let $g_1,\dots,g_n$ be unipotent automorphisms of two-dimensional vector spaces over a field of characteristic $0$, each consisting of a single Jordan block. Then $g_1\otimes\cdots\otimes g_n$ is unipotent, and
\[
\mathrm{U}(2)^{\otimes n}\cong\bigoplus_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}m_{n,k}\,\mathrm{U}(n-2k+1).
\]
In particular $g_1\otimes\cdots\otimes g_n$ has $\binom n{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ Jordan blocks, which is the dimension of its fixed space. The number of blocks of size $1$ is the Catalan number $m_{n,n/2}$ if $n$ is even, and $0$ if $n$ is odd.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For a unipotent automorphism $g$, the logarithm $N=\log g$ is a nilpotent endomorphism with the same Jordan type: $g-1=N\,e(N)$, where $e(N)=1+N/2+\cdots$ is invertible and commutes with $N$. The factors $1\otimes\cdots\otimes g_i\otimes\cdots\otimes1$ commute, so $\log(g_1\otimes\cdots\otimes g_n)=\sum_iN_i$ with $N_i=1\otimes\cdots\otimes\log g_i\otimes\cdots\otimes1$. In bases in which every $\log g_i$ is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, the endomorphism $\sum_iN_i$ is the action of $e=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\mathfrak{sl}_2$ on the $n$-th tensor power of the standard representation $\mathrm{St}$. On an irreducible $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-module of dimension $d$ the element $e$ is a single Jordan block of size $d$. So the Jordan type is the multiset of dimensions of the irreducible constituents of $\mathrm{St}^{\otimes n}$. By the Clebsch--Gordan rule, $\mathrm{St}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^{d}\cong\operatorname{Sym}^{d+1}\oplus\operatorname{Sym}^{d-1}$ for $d\ge1$ and $\mathrm{St}\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^0=\mathrm{St}$. Hence the multiplicity $\mu_{n,k}$ of $\operatorname{Sym}^{n-2k}$ in $\mathrm{St}^{\otimes n}$ satisfies $\mu_{1,0}=1$ and $\mu_{n,k}=\mu_{n-1,k}+\mu_{n-1,k-1}$ for $0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, where $\mu_{n-1,-1}=0$ and, for even $n$, $\mu_{n-1,n/2}=0$. The numbers $m_{n,k}$ satisfy the same recursion and initial value. Indeed, by Pascal's rule both $m_{n-1,k}+m_{n-1,k-1}$ and $m_{n,k}$ equal $\binom{n-1}k-\binom{n-1}{k-2}$, and $m_{n-1,n/2}=0$ for even $n$. Hence $\mu_{n,k}=m_{n,k}$. The number of blocks telescopes to $\binom n{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, and the blocks of size $1$ correspond to $k=n/2$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:frob-block}
Let $x$ be an $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational point of a smooth curve over $\mathbb{F}_q$, let $D_x$ be a decomposition group at $x$, with inertia group $I_x$ and wild inertia group $I^{\mathrm{w}}_x$, and let $\gamma\in I_x$ be an element whose image topologically generates $I_x/I^{\mathrm{w}}_x$. Let $\phi\in D_x$ induce the geometric Frobenius $z\mapsto z^{1/q}$ on $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q$. Let $V$ be a two-dimensional continuous representation of $D_x$ on which $I^{\mathrm{w}}_x$ acts trivially and $\gamma$ acts by a unipotent automorphism $T\ne1$, and suppose that $\phi$ acts trivially on the line $V^{I_x}$. Put $N=\log T$. Then there is a basis $e_1,e_2$ of $V$ with $Ne_1=0$, $Ne_2=e_1$, $\phi e_1=e_1$ and $\phi e_2=qe_2$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $\varpi$ be a uniformizer at $x$. The tame quotient $I_x/I^{\mathrm{w}}_x$ is identified with $\varprojlim_{p\nmid m}\mu_m(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q)$ by $\sigma\mapsto\big(\sigma(\varpi^{1/m})/\varpi^{1/m}\big)_m$; this does not depend on the choice of the roots $\varpi^{1/m}$. Let $\sigma\in I_x$, let $m$ be prime to $p$, and put $\zeta=\sigma(\varpi^{1/m})/\varpi^{1/m}$. Write $\phi^{-1}(\varpi^{1/m})=\xi\varpi^{1/m}$ with $\xi\in\mu_m(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q)$, so that $\phi(\varpi^{1/m})=\phi(\xi)^{-1}\varpi^{1/m}$. Since $\sigma$ acts trivially on $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q$,
\[
\phi\sigma\phi^{-1}(\varpi^{1/m})=\phi(\xi\zeta\varpi^{1/m})=\phi(\zeta)\,\varpi^{1/m}=\zeta^{1/q}\varpi^{1/m}.
\]
Thus conjugation by $\phi$ induces on $I_x/I^{\mathrm{w}}_x$ the inverse of the $q$-th power map, which is multiplication by $q^{-1}$ in the procyclic group $I_x/I^{\mathrm{w}}_x\cong\prod_{\ell'\ne p}\mathbb Z_{\ell'}$. The action of $I_x$ on $V$ factors through $I_x/I^{\mathrm{w}}_x$, and the closure of the group generated by $T$ is $\exp(\mathbb Z_\ell N)$; so $\gamma^a$ acts by $\exp(a_\ell N)$, where $a_\ell$ is the component of $a\in\prod_{\ell'\ne p}\mathbb Z_{\ell'}$ in $\mathbb Z_\ell$. Hence $F=\phi|_V$ satisfies $FTF^{-1}=\exp(q^{-1}N)$, and taking logarithms, $FNF^{-1}=q^{-1}N$, that is, $NF=qFN$.

As $T\ne1$ is unipotent on a space of dimension two, $N=T-1$ is nonzero with $N^2=0$, and $\ker N=V^{I_x}$ is a line, spanned by a vector $e_1$ with $Fe_1=e_1$. Choose $v$ with $Nv=e_1$. Then $N(Fv)=qFNv=qe_1=N(qv)$, so $Fv=qv+ce_1$ for some scalar $c$. Since $q\ne1$, the vector $e_2=v+(q-1)^{-1}ce_1$ satisfies $Fe_2=qe_2$ and $Ne_2=e_1$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:semisimple}
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $H$ is a linear algebraic group over $k$ with $H^0$ reductive, every finite-dimensional representation of $H$ is semisimple.
\item If $H\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is a Zariski-closed subgroup and $V$ is a semisimple representation of $H$, then $H^0$ is reductive.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
(i) In characteristic $0$, every finite-dimensional representation of a connected reductive group is semisimple. Let $U$ be a finite-dimensional representation of $H$, let $W\subseteq U$ be an $H$-stable subspace, and let $\varpi\colon U\to W$ be an $H^0$-equivariant projection. For $g\in H$ the map $g\varpi g^{-1}$ is again a projection onto $W$, and it depends only on the coset $gH^0$. The average of the $g\varpi g^{-1}$ over the finite group $H/H^0$ is therefore an $H$-equivariant projection onto $W$, and its kernel is an $H$-stable complement of $W$.

(ii) The unipotent radical $R_u(H^0)$ is a normal unipotent subgroup of $H$. It has a nonzero fixed vector in each simple summand of $V$, and these fixed vectors form an $H$-stable subspace of the summand, hence the whole summand. So $R_u(H^0)$ acts trivially on $V$, and it is trivial because $V$ is a faithful representation of $H$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:averages}
Let $T$ be a smooth geometrically connected variety of dimension $d$ over a finite field $\mathbb F_{q_0}$, and let $\mathcal E$ be a lisse sheaf on $T$, pointwise pure of weight $0$, with geometric generic stalk $V_{\mathcal E}$. Let $\pi^{\mathrm g}=\pi_1(T\otimes\overline{\mathbb F}_{q_0})$, and let $M$ be the dimension of the space of invariants $V_{\mathcal E}^{\pi^{\mathrm g}}$. Then $\operatorname{Frob}_{q_0}$ acts on $V_{\mathcal E}^{\pi^{\mathrm g}}$ with eigenvalues $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_M$ of absolute value $1$, and for $q=q_0^k$
\[
q^{-d}\sum_{x\in T(\mathbb{F}_q)}\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_x\mid\mathcal E)=\sum_{m=1}^M\beta_m^k+O\big(q^{-1/2}\big),
\]
where the implied constant depends only on $\mathcal E$. Consequently, if the left-hand side converges to a limit $L$ as $k\to\infty$, then $L=M$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
By the Grothendieck--Lefschetz trace formula \cite[Rapport]{SGA45}, the left-hand side is $q^{-d}\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{Tr}\big(\operatorname{Frob}_q\mid H^i_c(T\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal E)\big)$. Here $H^i_c(T\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal E)=0$ for $i>2d$. For $i<2d$ the group $H^i_c$ is mixed of weights at most $i\le2d-1$ \cite[Th.~3.3.1]{Deligne}, so every eigenvalue of $\operatorname{Frob}_q$ on it has absolute value at most $q^{d-1/2}$; its dimension does not depend on $k$. Hence these terms contribute at most $q^{-1/2}\sum_{i<2d}\dim H^i_c(T\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal E)$. Moreover $H^{2d}_c(T\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal E)\cong(V_{\mathcal E})_{\pi^{\mathrm g}}(-d)$. The fundamental group $\pi_1(T)$ acts on $V_{\mathcal E}$, and its normal subgroup $\pi^{\mathrm g}$ acts semisimply, because $\mathcal E$ is pure and hence geometrically semisimple \cite[3.4.1(iii)]{Deligne}. So the natural map $V_{\mathcal E}^{\pi^{\mathrm g}}\to(V_{\mathcal E})_{\pi^{\mathrm g}}$ is an isomorphism, compatible with the action of $\pi_1(T)/\pi^{\mathrm g}=\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q/\mathbb F_{q_0})$. By Poincar\'e duality, $H^{2d}_c(T\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal E)$ is dual to $H^0(T\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal E^\vee)(d)$, and $H^0(T\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal E^\vee)$ embeds into the stalk of $\mathcal E^\vee$ at a geometric point above a closed point, compatibly with the Frobenius of that point. Hence $H^{2d}_c$ is pure of weight $2d$, and the $\beta_m$ have absolute value $1$. This proves the formula. If its left-hand side converges to $L$, then $\sum_m\beta_m^k\to L$. By Dirichlet's simultaneous approximation theorem there are infinitely many $k$ for which every $\beta_m^k$ is arbitrarily close to $1$; along them $\sum_m\beta_m^k\to M$, and hence $L=M$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:faces}
Let $\varphi\ne0$ and $M=M_\varphi$.
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item $\beta-M\le\xi_i\le M$ for every $i$, $\beta\le M$, and $\beta\le2M$.
\item If $\beta=2M$, then $M<0$, $\varphi=-M\varphi^*$, and $P_n^\varphi=\sigma^*$.
\item If $\beta\ne2M$, each index $i$ is of exactly one of the types
\[
\mathrm A:\ \xi_i=M,\qquad\mathrm B:\ \xi_i=\beta-M,\qquad\mathrm N:\ \beta-M<\xi_i<M.
\]
The face $P_n^\varphi$ is the convex hull of the $\mathbf a_i$ with $i$ of type $\mathrm A$, the $\mathbf b_i$ with $i$ of type $\mathrm B$, and, if and only if $\beta=M$, the point $\mathbf c$. If $\beta<M$, some index is not of type $\mathrm N$.
\item Conversely, let $J_{\mathrm A},J_{\mathrm B}\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ be disjoint and $\eta\in\{0,1\}$, with $J_{\mathrm A}\cup J_{\mathrm B}\ne\varnothing$ if $\eta=0$. Let $\tau(J_{\mathrm A},J_{\mathrm B},\eta)$ be the convex hull of $\{\mathbf a_i\}_{i\in J_{\mathrm A}}\cup\{\mathbf b_j\}_{j\in J_{\mathrm B}}$, together with $\mathbf c$ if $\eta=1$. Then there is a $\varphi$ with $M_\varphi=1$ and $P_n^\varphi=\tau(J_{\mathrm A},J_{\mathrm B},\eta)$.
\item The vertex set of $\tau(J_{\mathrm A},J_{\mathrm B},\eta)$ is linearly independent. In particular $\tau(J_{\mathrm A},J_{\mathrm B},\eta)$ is a simplex of dimension $|J_{\mathrm A}|+|J_{\mathrm B}|+\eta-1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
(a) The values $\xi_i$, $\beta-\xi_i$ and $\beta$ are at most $M$; adding the first two for $i=1$ gives $\beta\le2M$.

(b) If $\beta=2M$, then $\beta-M=M$, so (a) forces $\xi_i=M$ for all $i$. Thus $\alpha=-M(1,\dots,1)$ and $\beta=2M$, that is, $\varphi=-M\varphi^*$. Since $\varphi\ne0$ we have $M\ne0$, and $2M=\beta\le M$ gives $M<0$. Every $\mathbf a_i$ and every $\mathbf b_i$ takes the value $M$, whereas $\varphi(\mathbf c)=2M<M$; hence $P_n^\varphi=\sigma^*$.

(c) If $\beta\ne2M$, then $\beta<2M$ by (a), so $\beta-M<M$. By (a), $\xi_i$ lies in $[\beta-M,M]$ and equals at most one of its endpoints. Since $\mathbf a_i\in P_n^\varphi$ if and only if $\xi_i=M$, $\mathbf b_i\in P_n^\varphi$ if and only if $\xi_i=\beta-M$, and $\mathbf c\in P_n^\varphi$ if and only if $\beta=M$, the description of the face follows. If $\beta<M$ and every index were of type $\mathrm N$, no generator would attain the value $M$.

(d) For $\eta=0$ take $\beta=0$, and $\alpha_i=-1$, $1$ or $0$ according as $i\in J_{\mathrm A}$, $i\in J_{\mathrm B}$ or $i\notin J_{\mathrm A}\cup J_{\mathrm B}$. Then $\varphi(\mathbf a_i)$ is $1$, $-1$ or $0$, $\varphi(\mathbf b_i)$ is $-1$, $1$ or $0$, and $\varphi(\mathbf c)=0$. Since $J_{\mathrm A}\cup J_{\mathrm B}\ne\varnothing$, the maximum is $1$, attained exactly at the vertices of $\tau(J_{\mathrm A},J_{\mathrm B},0)$. For $\eta=1$ take $\beta=1$, and $\alpha_i=-1$, $0$ or $-\frac12$ according as $i\in J_{\mathrm A}$, $i\in J_{\mathrm B}$ or $i\notin J_{\mathrm A}\cup J_{\mathrm B}$. Then $\varphi(\mathbf a_i)$ is $1$, $0$ or $\frac12$, $\varphi(\mathbf b_i)$ is $0$, $1$ or $\frac12$, and $\varphi(\mathbf c)=1$, so the maximum $1$ is attained exactly at the vertices of $\tau(J_{\mathrm A},J_{\mathrm B},1)$.

(e) In a linear relation $\sum_{i\in J_{\mathrm A}}c_i\mathbf a_i+\sum_{j\in J_{\mathrm B}}d_j\mathbf b_j+c_0\mathbf c=0$, the coordinate $x_i$ with $i\in J_{\mathrm A}$ receives only the contribution $-c_i$, and the coordinate $x_j$ with $j\in J_{\mathrm B}$ only the contribution $d_j$. Hence all $c_i$ and $d_j$ vanish, and then $c_0=0$. Linearly independent points are affinely independent.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:structure}
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $\dim P_n=n+1$, and $0\notin P_n$.
\item $\sigma^*$ is a facet of $P_n$; it is cut out by $\varphi^*$, which takes the value $-1$ on it. With $\mathbf m=\frac12\mathbf c$ and $w_i=e_i+\frac12e_{n+1}$ one has $\sigma^*=\mathbf m+\operatorname{conv}\{\pm w_1,\dots,\pm w_n\}$, and $w_1,\dots,w_n$ are linearly independent. Thus $\sigma^*$ is an $n$-dimensional cross-polytope; for $n\ge2$ it has $2n>n+1$ vertices and is not a simplex.
\item $P_n=\operatorname{conv}(\sigma^*\cup\{\mathbf c\})$ and $\Delta_n=P_n\cup\operatorname{conv}(\sigma^*\cup\{0\})$. These two pyramids over $\sigma^*$ have disjoint interiors and equal volumes, so $\operatorname{Vol}(\Delta_n)=2\operatorname{Vol}(P_n)$.
\item The proper faces of $P_n$ are $\sigma^*$ and the pairwise distinct simplices $\tau(J_{\mathrm A},J_{\mathrm B},\eta)$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:faces}(d). Consequently, for $0\le j\le n$,
\[
f_j(P_n)=\binom n{j+1}2^{j+1}+\binom nj2^j+[\,j=n\,],
\]
where $[\,j=n\,]$ is $1$ if $j=n$ and $0$ otherwise. For $n=4$ the $f$-vector $(f_0,\dots,f_4)$ of the $5$-dimensional polytope $P_4$ is $(9,32,56,48,17)$.
\item The faces of $\Delta_n$ not containing $0$ are exactly the proper faces of $P_n$ other than $\sigma^*$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
(i) The differences $\mathbf b_i-\mathbf c=e_i$ ($1\le i\le n$) and $(\mathbf c-\mathbf a_1)-(\mathbf b_1-\mathbf c)=e_{n+1}$ span $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, so the affine hull of $P_n$ is $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The coordinate $y$ vanishes at the $\mathbf a_i$ and equals $1$ at the $\mathbf b_i$ and at $\mathbf c$. If $0$ were a convex combination of the generators, the coefficients of the $\mathbf b_i$ and of $\mathbf c$ would vanish, and $0$ would be a convex combination of $-e_1,\dots,-e_n$, which is absurd.

(ii) For $\varphi^*$ we have $\xi_i=-1$ and $\beta=-2$; so $\max_{P_n}\varphi^*=-1$ and, by Theorem~\ref{thm:faces}(b), $\varphi^*$ cuts out $\sigma^*$. All segments $[\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i]$ have midpoint $\mathbf m$, and $\mathbf b_i-\mathbf m=w_i=-(\mathbf a_i-\mathbf m)$. The $w_i$ are linearly independent, since their first $n$ coordinates form the identity matrix. Hence the affine hull of $\sigma^*$ is $\mathbf m+\sum_i\mathbb Rw_i$, of dimension $n=\dim P_n-1$, and $\sigma^*$ is the image of the standard cross-polytope $\operatorname{conv}\{\pm e_1,\dots,\pm e_n\}\subset\mathbb R^n$ under the affine embedding $z\mapsto\mathbf m+\sum_iz_iw_i$.

(iii) Every generator of $P_n$ other than $\mathbf c$ lies in $\sigma^*$, so $P_n=\operatorname{conv}(\sigma^*\cup\{\mathbf c\})$. Since $\mathbf c=2\mathbf m$, a point of $\operatorname{conv}(\sigma^*\cup\{0,\mathbf c\})$ can be written $z=(1-a-b)s+b\,\mathbf c$ with $s\in\sigma^*$, $a,b\ge0$ and $a+b\le1$. If $a\ge b$, then $z=(1-a-b)s+2b\,\mathbf m+(a-b)\cdot0$ is a convex combination of points of $\sigma^*$ and of $0$. If $b\ge a$, then $z=(1-a-b)s+2a\,\mathbf m+(b-a)\mathbf c$ is a convex combination of points of $\sigma^*$ and of $\mathbf c$. Hence $\Delta_n$ is the union of the two pyramids. They lie on the two sides $\{\varphi^*\le-1\}$ and $\{\varphi^*\ge-1\}$ of the hyperplane spanned by $\sigma^*$, so their interiors are disjoint. Since $\varphi^*(\mathbf c)=-2$ and $\varphi^*(0)=0$, the two apices are at the same distance from that hyperplane, and the pyramids have the same volume.

(iv) By Theorem~\ref{thm:faces}(b),(c), every proper face is $\sigma^*$ or of the form $\tau(J_{\mathrm A},J_{\mathrm B},\eta)$, and by Theorem~\ref{thm:faces}(d) each such $\tau$ is a face. Distinct data $(J_{\mathrm A},J_{\mathrm B},\eta)$ give distinct vertex sets, and $\sigma^*$ contains both $\mathbf a_1$ and $\mathbf b_1$, which no $\tau$ does. By Theorem~\ref{thm:faces}(e) the simplex $\tau(J_{\mathrm A},J_{\mathrm B},\eta)$ has dimension $j=|J_{\mathrm A}|+|J_{\mathrm B}|+\eta-1$. For $\eta=0$ there are $\binom n{j+1}2^{j+1}$ choices with $|J_{\mathrm A}|+|J_{\mathrm B}|=j+1$ (choose the indices, then a type for each), and for $\eta=1$ there are $\binom nj2^j$; the facet $\sigma^*$ contributes $[\,j=n\,]$.

(v) Let $\tau$ be a face of $\Delta_n$ with $0\notin\tau$, cut out by a linear form $\varphi$ with maximum $M'$ on $\Delta_n$. Then $M'>\varphi(0)=0$, and since $\Delta_n=\operatorname{conv}(P_n\cup\{0\})$, we get $M'=M_\varphi$ and $\tau=P_n^\varphi$. This is a proper face of $P_n$ (as $\varphi$ is not constant on $P_n$) cut out by a form with positive maximum. By Theorem~\ref{thm:faces}(b) every form cutting out $\sigma^*$ has negative maximum, so $\tau\ne\sigma^*$. Conversely, every proper face of $P_n$ other than $\sigma^*$ is cut out by a form $\varphi$ with $M_\varphi=1$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:faces}(d)), and this form cuts out the same face of $\Delta_n$, because $\varphi(0)=0<1$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:volume}
For $J\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ let
\[
\tau_J=\operatorname{conv}\big(\{0,\mathbf c\}\cup\{\mathbf a_i\}_{i\in J}\cup\{\mathbf b_j\}_{j\notin J}\big).
\]
Each $\tau_J$ is a unimodular $(n+1)$-simplex, $\Delta_n=\bigcup_J\tau_J$, and the interiors of the $\tau_J$ are pairwise disjoint. Consequently
\[
(n+1)!\,\operatorname{Vol}(\Delta_n)=2^n,\qquad(n+1)!\,\operatorname{Vol}(P_n)=2^{n-1}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The edge vectors of $\tau_J$ at the vertex $0$ are $-e_i$ ($i\in J$), $e_j+e_{n+1}$ ($j\notin J$) and $e_{n+1}$. Subtracting the last vector from those of the second group turns them into a signed permutation of the standard basis, so $\tau_J$ is a unimodular simplex. Write a point of $\tau_J$ as $\sum_{i\in J}\beta_i\mathbf a_i+\sum_{j\notin J}\delta_j\mathbf b_j+\gamma\mathbf c+\alpha\cdot0$, with nonnegative coefficients of sum $1$. Then $x_i=-\beta_i$ ($i\in J$), $x_j=\delta_j$ ($j\notin J$), $y=\gamma+\sum_{j\notin J}\delta_j$ and $\alpha=1+\sum_{i\in J}x_i-y$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tauJ}
\tau_J=\Big\{(x,y):\ x_i\le0\ (i\in J),\ \ x_j\ge0\ (j\notin J),\ \ \sum_{j\notin J}x_j\le y\le1+\sum_{i\in J}x_i\Big\}.
\end{equation}
Let $K=\{(x,y):\sum_ix_i^+\le y\le1-\sum_ix_i^-\}$, where $x^{\pm}=\max(\pm x,0)$. The set $K$ is convex, because $x\mapsto\sum_ix_i^{\pm}$ are convex functions. It contains $0$, $\mathbf c$, every $\mathbf a_i$ (for which $0\le0\le1-1$) and every $\mathbf b_i$ (for which $1\le1\le1$); hence $\Delta_n\subseteq K$. Conversely, given $(x,y)\in K$ put $J=\{i:x_i<0\}$; then \eqref{eq:tauJ} shows $(x,y)\in\tau_J\subseteq\Delta_n$. Thus $\Delta_n=K=\bigcup_J\tau_J$. If $J\ne J'$ and $i$ lies in exactly one of them, then the interior of one of $\tau_J,\tau_{J'}$ lies in $\{x_i<0\}$ and that of the other in $\{x_i>0\}$. A unimodular $(n+1)$-simplex has volume $1/(n+1)!$, which gives the first formula; the second follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:structure}(iii).
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:euclidean}
The volumes can also be computed from the cross-polytope. The Gram matrix of the vectors $w_1,\dots,w_n$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:structure}(ii) is $\mathrm I_n+\frac14\mathrm J_n$, where $\mathrm J_n$ is the all-ones matrix. Its eigenvalues are $1+\frac n4$, once, and $1$, with multiplicity $n-1$, so its determinant is $\frac{n+4}4$. The standard cross-polytope in $\mathbb R^n$ has volume $2^n/n!$. Hence the $n$-dimensional Euclidean volume of the facet $\sigma^*$ is
\[
\operatorname{Vol}_n(\sigma^*)=\frac{2^n}{n!}\sqrt{\frac{n+4}4}.
\]
The facet lies in the hyperplane $\varphi^*=-1$, whose normal vector $(1,\dots,1,-2)$ has length $\sqrt{n+4}$, and $\varphi^*(\mathbf c)=-2$. So the apex $\mathbf c$ is at distance $1/\sqrt{n+4}$ from this hyperplane, and
\[
\operatorname{Vol}(P_n)=\frac1{n+1}\cdot\frac{2^n}{n!}\sqrt{\frac{n+4}4}\cdot\frac1{\sqrt{n+4}}=\frac{2^{n-1}}{(n+1)!},
\]
in agreement with Proposition~\ref{prop:volume}. For $n=4$, $\operatorname{Vol}_4(\sigma^*)=\frac23\sqrt2$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:nondeg}
Let $h\in(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^\times)^n$. For every face $\tau$ of $\Delta_n$ not containing $0$, the partial derivatives of the face polynomial $F_{n,\tau}$, the sum of the monomials of $F_n$ whose exponents lie in $\tau$, have no common zero on the torus $\mathbb{G}_m^{n+1}$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$. Thus $F_n$ is non-degenerate with respect to $\Delta_n$ in the sense of \cite{AS}, and $\dim\Delta_n=n+1$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:structure}(iv),(v), $\tau=\tau(J_{\mathrm A},J_{\mathrm B},\eta)$ with $J_{\mathrm A}\cap J_{\mathrm B}=\varnothing$. If $i\in J_{\mathrm A}$, then $i\notin J_{\mathrm B}$, so the only monomial of $F_{n,\tau}$ involving $u_i$ is $u_i^{-1}$, and $\partial F_{n,\tau}/\partial u_i=-u_i^{-2}$ does not vanish on the torus. If $J_{\mathrm A}=\varnothing$ and $j\in J_{\mathrm B}$, then $\partial F_{n,\tau}/\partial u_j=h_jt\ne0$. If $J_{\mathrm A}=J_{\mathrm B}=\varnothing$, then $F_{n,\tau}=\lambda t$, and $\partial F_{n,\tau}/\partial t=\lambda\ne0$. Finally $\dim\Delta_n=n+1$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:structure}(i).
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:crit}
Let $h\in(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^\times)^n$, fix $s_i\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ with $s_i^2=h_i$, and for $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}^n$ put $L_\varepsilon=\sum_i\varepsilon_is_i$. The critical points of $F_n(\cdot,\cdot;h)$ on $\mathbb{G}_m^n\times\mathbb{G}_m$ are in bijection with the pairs $\{\varepsilon,-\varepsilon\}$ such that $L_\varepsilon\ne0$; the pair $\{\pm\varepsilon\}$ corresponds to the point
\[
u_i=-\frac{\lambda\varepsilon_i}{s_iL_\varepsilon},\qquad t=\frac{L_\varepsilon^2}{\lambda^2}.
\]
At each critical point, $\det\operatorname{Hess}F_n=2^{n-1}\lambda/(t\,u_1^3\cdots u_n^3)\ne0$. In particular, on the dense open subset $\Omega_n\subset\mathbb{G}_m^n$ where $\prod_\varepsilon L_\varepsilon\ne0$, the phase has exactly $2^{n-1}$ critical points, all of them non-degenerate.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The critical equations are $u_i^{-2}=th_i$ ($1\le i\le n$) and $\lambda+\langle h,u\rangle=0$. Let $(u,t)$ be a critical point and $\tau$ a square root of $t$. Then $(s_i\tau u_i)^2=1$, so $\varepsilon_i:=s_i\tau u_i\in\{\pm1\}$ and $u_i=\varepsilon_i/(s_i\tau)$. The last equation becomes $\lambda+L_\varepsilon/\tau=0$, so $L_\varepsilon\ne0$ and $\tau=-L_\varepsilon/\lambda$. Replacing $\tau$ by $-\tau$ replaces $\varepsilon$ by $-\varepsilon$, so the critical point determines the pair $\{\pm\varepsilon\}$. Conversely, if $L_\varepsilon\ne0$, the displayed formulas define a critical point, and $\varepsilon$ and $-\varepsilon$ give the same point. If $\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon'$ give the same point, the corresponding square roots satisfy $\tau'=\pm\tau$, and hence $\varepsilon'=\pm\varepsilon$.

The Hessian in $(u_1,\dots,u_n,t)$ is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}D&h\\ h^{T}&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $D=\operatorname{diag}(2u_i^{-3})$. By the Schur complement formula its determinant is $-\det(D)\,h^{T}D^{-1}h=-\frac{2^n}{\prod_iu_i^3}\cdot\frac12\sum_ih_i^2u_i^3$. At a critical point $h_i=u_i^{-2}t^{-1}$, so $h_i^2u_i^3=t^{-2}u_i^{-1}$ and $u_i^{-1}=th_iu_i$. Therefore $\sum_ih_i^2u_i^3=t^{-1}\langle h,u\rangle=-\lambda/t$, and the determinant equals $2^{n-1}\lambda/(t\prod_iu_i^3)$, which is nonzero because $p$ is odd. The open set $\Omega_n$ is dense: the product $\prod_\varepsilon L_\varepsilon$ is invariant under all sign changes of the $s_i$, hence a polynomial in $h$, and it is nonzero because its coefficient of $h_1^{2^{n-1}}$ is $\pm1$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:critical-values}
At the critical point attached to $\{\pm\varepsilon\}$ the constraint $\lambda+\langle h,u\rangle=0$ holds, so the critical value is $f(u)=\sum_iu_i^{-1}=-\lambda^{-1}L_\varepsilon\sum_i\varepsilon_is_i=-L_\varepsilon^2/\lambda$. Since $\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}^n}L_\varepsilon^2=\sum_{i,j}s_is_j\sum_\varepsilon\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j=2^n\sum_ih_i$, the sum of the critical values over the $2^{n-1}$ critical points, for $h\in\Omega_n$, is
\[
-\frac1\lambda\sum_{\{\pm\varepsilon\}}L_\varepsilon^2=-\frac{2^{n-1}}\lambda\,(h_1+\cdots+h_n).
\]
This is the function in Theorem~\ref{thmE}(i). The identity of Theorem~\ref{thmE}(i) holds on all of $S$, although critical points escape to infinity along the divisors $L_\varepsilon=0$ (Remark~\ref{rem:collision}); along them the critical value of the escaping point, $-L_\varepsilon^2/\lambda$, tends to $0$. The proof of Theorem~\ref{thmE}(i) does not use critical points.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:AS}
(a) By Propositions~\ref{prop:nondeg} and~\ref{prop:volume}, the theorems of Adolphson--Sperber \cite{AS} and Denef--Loeser \cite{DL} predict that $H^i_c(\mathbb{G}_m^{n+1}\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mathcal{L}_\psi(F_n))$ vanishes for $i\ne n+1$ and has dimension $(n+1)!\operatorname{Vol}(\Delta_n)=2^n$; we prove this directly in Proposition~\ref{prop:fibration}. The origin is a vertex of $\Delta_n$, not an interior point, so the purity criterion of \cite{AS,DL} does not apply, and indeed the cohomology is mixed (Proposition~\ref{prop:weights-torus}).

(b) The face $\sigma^*$ of $P_n$ is not a face of $\Delta_n$, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:nondeg} it is the only proper face of $P_n$ at which non-degeneracy can fail. Its face polynomial is $\sum_i(u_i^{-1}+h_itu_i)$. The computation in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:crit} shows that the partial derivatives of this polynomial have a common zero on the torus if and only if $L_\varepsilon=0$ for some $\varepsilon$. On $\Omega_n$ the phase is therefore non-degenerate with respect to every proper face of $P_n$. The count $2^{n-1}$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:crit} is the one predicted by Bernstein's theorem \cite{Bernstein}. Indeed, the critical points are the common zeros on the torus of the $n+1$ Laurent polynomials
\[
u_i\frac{\partial F_n}{\partial u_i}=-u_i^{-1}+h_itu_i\quad(1\le i\le n),\qquad t\frac{\partial F_n}{\partial t}=t\big(\lambda+\langle h,u\rangle\big),
\]
whose Newton polytopes are the segments $[\mathbf a_i,\mathbf b_i]$ and the simplex $Q=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf c,\mathbf b_1,\dots,\mathbf b_n\}$. Normalize mixed volumes in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ so that $n+1$ copies of a polytope $P$ have mixed volume $(n+1)!\operatorname{Vol}(P)$. As the first $n$ polytopes are segments with directions $v_i=\mathbf b_i-\mathbf a_i=2e_i+e_{n+1}$, their mixed volume with $Q$ is $\max_{y,y'\in Q}|\det(v_1,\dots,v_n,y-y')|$. The linear form $w\mapsto\det(v_1,\dots,v_n,w)$ and the form $\varphi^*$ both vanish on the hyperplane spanned by the linearly independent vectors $v_i$, so they are proportional. Expanding $\det(v_1,\dots,v_n,e_1)=-2^{n-1}$ along its last column, and using $\varphi^*(e_1)=1$, gives $\det(v_1,\dots,v_n,w)=-2^{n-1}\varphi^*(w)$. Since $\varphi^*$ takes the value $-2$ at $\mathbf c$ and $-1$ at every $\mathbf b_i$, the mixed volume is $2^{n-1}$, which also equals $(n+1)!\operatorname{Vol}(P_n)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:volume}). The cohomology of the torus is twice as large because $\Delta_n$ contains the second pyramid $\operatorname{conv}(\sigma^*\cup\{0\})$. Nothing in this remark is used later.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:purity-example}
The failure of purity in Remark~\ref{rem:AS}(a) can be seen already in dimension one. Let $g(u)=u+u^2$ on $\mathbb{G}_m$. Its Newton polytope is $[1,2]$ and its Newton polyhedron at infinity is $[0,2]$, of normalized volume $2$, with $0$ as a vertex. The only face not containing $0$ is $\{2\}$, with face polynomial $u^2$, whose derivative $2u$ does not vanish on $\mathbb{G}_m$ because $p$ is odd; so $g$ is non-degenerate. The sheaf $\mathcal{L}_\psi(g)$ on $\mathbb A^1$ is lisse, with $\operatorname{Swan}_\infty=2$, so its compactly supported cohomology is concentrated in degree $1$ and is one-dimensional; it is pure of weight $1$ by \cite[3.2.3]{Deligne}, since $\mathcal{L}_\psi(g)$ is totally wild at $\infty$. As $g(0)=0$, excision for $\{0\}\subset\mathbb A^1$ gives an exact sequence
\[
0\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell\to H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_m\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(g))\to H^1_c(\mathbb A^1\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(g))\to0,
\]
with $\operatorname{Frob}_q$ acting trivially on $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$. Thus $H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_m\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(g))$ has dimension $2$, as predicted by \cite{AS}, and it is mixed, of weights $0$ and $1$. For the Kloosterman phase $u^{-1}+au$, by contrast, the polyhedron at infinity is $[-1,1]$, the origin is an interior point, and the cohomology is pure.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:fibration}
Let $\operatorname{pr}\colon X_h^\circ\to\mathbb{G}_{m,t}$ be the projection and
\[
\mathcal N_h=\Big(\bigotimes_{i=1}^n[\times h_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}\Big)\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t).
\]
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $R\operatorname{pr}_!\mathcal L\cong\mathcal N_h[-n]$, and $\mathcal N_h$ is lisse of rank $2^n$ on $\mathbb{G}_m$ and pure of weight $n$.
\item $\mathcal N_h$ is tame at $0$, with $\mathcal N_h(0)\cong\mathrm{U}(2)^{\otimes n}$, and totally wild at $\infty$, with all breaks equal to $1$. Hence $\operatorname{Swan}_0(\mathcal N_h)=0$ and $\operatorname{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal N_h)=2^n$.
\item $H^i_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathcal N_h)=0$ for $i\ne1$, and $\dim H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathcal N_h)=2^n$. Consequently $H^i_c(X_h^\circ,\mathcal L)\cong H^{i-n}_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathcal N_h)$ vanishes for $i\ne n+1$ and has dimension $2^n$ for $i=n+1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
(i) Since $F_n=\lambda t+\sum_i(u_i^{-1}+h_itu_i)$, we have $\mathcal L\cong\operatorname{pr}^*\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t)\otimes\bigotimes_i\mathcal{L}_\psi(u_i^{-1}+h_itu_i)$, the $i$-th factor being pulled back from $\mathbb{G}_{m,u_i}\times\mathbb{G}_{m,t}$. By (K4) and proper base change along $t\mapsto h_it$, the direct image of $\mathcal{L}_\psi(u_i^{-1}+h_itu_i)$ to $\mathbb{G}_{m,t}$ is $[\times h_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}[-1]$. The K\"unneth formula over $\mathbb{G}_{m,t}$ and the projection formula give $R\operatorname{pr}_!\mathcal L\cong\mathcal N_h[-n]$. The remaining assertions of (i) follow from (K1).

(ii) By (K2) and \S\ref{sec:conventions}, each $[\times h_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}$ is tame at $0$ with local monodromy $\mathrm{U}(2)$, and $\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t)$ is lisse at $0$; the tame generator acts on the tensor product by the tensor product of its actions. At $\infty$ each $[\times h_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}$ has both breaks in $(0,1)$ by (K3), so their tensor product has all breaks $<1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:breaks}(i). Since $\lambda\ne0$, the sheaf $\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t)$ is isoclinic of break $1$ at $\infty$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:breaks}(ii) shows that $\mathcal N_h$ is isoclinic of break $1$ there.

(iii) By \eqref{eq:GOS}, $\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathcal N_h)=-2^n$. Moreover $H^0_c=0$, and $H^2_c=0$ because $\mathcal N_h$ is totally wild at $\infty$. The last assertion follows from (i) and the Leray spectral sequence of $\operatorname{pr}$, which degenerates.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:weights-torus}
Let $j\colon\mathbb{G}_m\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^1$ be the inclusion. There is an exact sequence of $\operatorname{Frob}_q$-modules
\[
0\longrightarrow\mathcal N_h^{I_0}\longrightarrow H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathcal N_h)\longrightarrow H^1(\mathbb P^1,j_*\mathcal N_h)\longrightarrow0,
\]
where $\mathcal N_h^{I_0}=(j_*\mathcal N_h)_0$ carries the action of the Frobenius at the rational point $0$. The right-hand term is pure of weight $n+1$ and has dimension $r(n)$. For $0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, exactly $m_{n,k}$ of the Frobenius eigenvalues on $\mathcal N_h^{I_0}$, counted with multiplicity, have weight $2k$, and there are no others. In particular $H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathcal N_h)$ contains a unique Frobenius-stable line of weight $0$ and has no other eigenvalue of weight $0$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The adjunction map $j_!\mathcal N_h\to j_*\mathcal N_h$ is injective, with cokernel the skyscraper sheaves $\mathcal N_h^{I_0}$ at $0$ and $\mathcal N_h^{I_\infty}$ at $\infty$; the latter vanishes because $\mathcal N_h$ is totally wild at $\infty$. Since $H^0(\mathbb P^1,j_*\mathcal N_h)=H^0(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathcal N_h)$ is contained in $\mathcal N_h^{I_\infty}=0$, and skyscraper sheaves have no $H^1$, the long exact cohomology sequence gives the displayed sequence, with $H^1(\mathbb P^1,j_!\mathcal N_h)=H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathcal N_h)$. By Deligne's theorem \cite[3.2.3]{Deligne}, $H^1(\mathbb P^1,j_*\mathcal N_h)$ is pure of weight $n+1$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:fibration}(ii) and Lemma~\ref{lem:CG}, the local monodromy of $\mathcal N_h$ at $0$ is unipotent, with $m_{n,k}$ Jordan blocks of size $n-2k+1$ for each $k$. So $\dim\mathcal N_h^{I_0}=\binom n{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, and the right-hand term has dimension $2^n-\binom n{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}=r(n)$. Finally, $\mathcal N_h$ is pure of weight $n$ with unipotent local monodromy at $0$. By Deligne's local monodromy theorem with weights \cite[1.8.4]{Deligne}, the monodromy filtration on the generic stalk, centred at $n$, has graded pieces $\operatorname{gr}^M_i$ pure of weight $n+i$; the invariants of a Jordan block of size $m$ lie in $M_{-(m-1)}$ and have weight $n-(m-1)$. A block of size $n-2k+1$ therefore contributes one eigenvalue of weight $2k$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:frob-invariants}
Let $h\in(\mathbb{F}_q^\times)^n$. Then $\operatorname{Frob}_q$ acts semisimply on $\mathcal N_h^{I_0}$, and its eigenvalues are the numbers $q^k$, $0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, with multiplicity $m_{n,k}$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Let $D_0$ be a decomposition group at the rational point $t=0$ of $\mathbb A^1$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, and let $I_0$, $I^{\mathrm{w}}_0$, $\gamma$ and $\phi$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:frob-block}, with $x=0$. For each $i$ let $V_i$ be the generic stalk of $[\times h_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}$, as a representation of $D_0$. By (K2) and \S\ref{sec:conventions}, $I^{\mathrm{w}}_0$ acts trivially on $V_i$ and $\gamma$ acts by a unipotent automorphism $T_i\ne1$. The map $t\mapsto h_it$ extends to an automorphism of $\mathbb A^1$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ fixing $0$, so $j_*[\times h_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}=[\times h_i]^*j_*\mathrm{Kl}$, and $V_i^{I_0}=(j_*\mathrm{Kl})_0$ as $\operatorname{Frob}_q$-modules. By (K5), $\phi$ acts trivially on $V_i^{I_0}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:frob-block} provides a basis $e^{(i)}_1,e^{(i)}_2$ of $V_i$ with $N_ie^{(i)}_1=0$, $N_ie^{(i)}_2=e^{(i)}_1$, $\phi e^{(i)}_1=e^{(i)}_1$ and $\phi e^{(i)}_2=qe^{(i)}_2$, where $N_i=\log T_i$.

The sheaf $\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t)$ is lisse at $0$, and $\phi$ acts on its stalk at $0$ by $\psi_q(0)=1$. So the generic stalk of $\mathcal N_h$ is $V=V_1\otimes\cdots\otimes V_n$ as a representation of $D_0$. On it $\gamma$ acts by $T_1\otimes\cdots\otimes T_n=\exp\big(\sum_iN_i\big)$, where $N_i$ acts on the $i$-th factor, and $\phi$ acts on the basis vectors $e_J=e^{(1)}_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e^{(n)}_{j_n}$ by $\phi e_J=q^{|J|}e_J$. As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:CG}, the invariants of $\exp(\sum_iN_i)$ form the kernel $E$ of $\sum_iN_i$, and in the basis $(e_J)$ the operator $\sum_iN_i$ is the one considered before~\eqref{eq:Ek}. Hence $\mathcal N_h^{I_0}=E=\bigoplus_kE_k$ with $\dim E_k=m_{n,k}$. Since $I_0$ is normal in $D_0$, the element $\phi$ preserves $E$; it also preserves the span of the $e_J$ with $|J|=k$, on which it acts as $q^k$. So $\phi$ acts on $E_k$ as multiplication by $q^k$. As $\phi$ induces $\operatorname{Frob}_q$ on $\mathcal N_h^{I_0}=(j_*\mathcal N_h)_0$, the proposition follows.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:t0}
$\mathcal L|_{Z_h}\cong\boxtimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal{L}_\psi(u_i^{-1})$. Its compactly supported cohomology vanishes outside degree $n$, and $H^n_c(Z_h,\mathcal L|_{Z_h})$ is one-dimensional, with $\operatorname{Frob}_q$ acting trivially.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Setting $t=0$ leaves the phase $\sum_iu_i^{-1}$. On $\mathbb{G}_m$, the sheaf $\mathcal{L}_\psi(u^{-1})$ is lisse of rank one, with $\operatorname{Swan}_0=1$ and $\operatorname{Swan}_\infty=0$. By \eqref{eq:GOS} its Euler characteristic is $-1$; its $H^0_c$ vanishes, and so does its $H^2_c$, because it is geometrically nontrivial. Hence its $H^1_c$ is one-dimensional, and the Grothendieck--Lefschetz formula $-\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_q\mid H^1_c)=\sum_{u\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times}\psi_q(u^{-1})=-1$ shows that $\operatorname{Frob}_q$ acts trivially on it. The K\"unneth formula concludes.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:fibre}
Let $n\ge2$ and $h\in(\mathbb{F}_q^\times)^n$.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $H^i_c(X_h,\mathcal L)=0$ for $i\ne n+1$.
\item The connecting homomorphism $\partial\colon H^n_c(Z_h,\mathcal L|_{Z_h})\to H^{n+1}_c(X_h^\circ,\mathcal L)$ of the excision sequence is injective, and its image is the unique line of weight $0$.
\item $\dim H^{n+1}_c(X_h,\mathcal L)=2^n-1$. The Frobenius eigenvalues are $r(n)$ eigenvalues of weight $n+1$ and, for $1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, the eigenvalue $q^k$ with multiplicity $m_{n,k}$. The subspace of weights $\le n$ is a direct sum of eigenspaces of $\operatorname{Frob}_q$.
\item $H^i_c(Y_h,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))=0$ for $i\ne n-1$, $H^{n-1}_c(Y_h,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))\cong H^{n+1}_c(X_h,\mathcal L)(1)$, and
\[
\Sigma_n(h)=(-1)^{n-1}\operatorname{Tr}\big(\operatorname{Frob}_q\mid H^{n-1}_c(Y_h,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))\big).
\]
The eigenvalues on $H^{n-1}_c(Y_h,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))$ are $r(n)$ of weight $n-1$ and, for $1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, the eigenvalue $q^{k-1}$ with multiplicity $m_{n,k}$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exact-formula}
\Sigma_n(h)=(-1)^{n-1}\Big(\tau_q(h)+\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}m_{n,k}\,q^{k-1}\Big),
\end{equation}
where $\tau_q(h)$ is the trace of $\operatorname{Frob}_q$ on the part of weight $n-1$, so that $|\tau_q(h)|\le r(n)q^{(n-1)/2}$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular Theorem~\ref{thmA} holds.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:integrate-t}, applied with $V=\mathbb{G}_m^n$, $g(u)=\lambda+\langle h,u\rangle$ and $K=\mathcal{L}_\psi(f)$, we have $H^i_c(X_h,\mathcal L)\cong H^{i-2}_c(Y_h,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))(-1)$ for all $i$. The variety $Y_h$ is smooth and affine of pure dimension $n-1$. By Artin's vanishing theorem \cite[Exp.~XIV]{SGA4} and Poincar\'e duality \cite[Exp.~XVIII]{SGA4}, $H^j_c(Y_h,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))=0$ for $j<n-1$. Hence $H^i_c(X_h,\mathcal L)=0$ for $i\le n$.

Consider the excision sequence
\[
\cdots\to H^i_c(X_h^\circ,\mathcal L)\to H^i_c(X_h,\mathcal L)\to H^i_c(Z_h,\mathcal L|_{Z_h})\xrightarrow{\ \partial\ }H^{i+1}_c(X_h^\circ,\mathcal L)\to\cdots.
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:fibration}(iii) and Lemma~\ref{lem:t0}, the groups $H^i_c(X_h^\circ,\mathcal L)$ and $H^i_c(Z_h,\mathcal L|_{Z_h})$ vanish except for $H^{n+1}_c(X_h^\circ,\mathcal L)$ and $H^n_c(Z_h,\mathcal L|_{Z_h})$. For $i\ge n+2$ this gives $H^i_c(X_h,\mathcal L)=0$, which proves (i), and the remaining part of the sequence reads
\[
0=H^n_c(X_h,\mathcal L)\to H^n_c(Z_h,\mathcal L|_{Z_h})\xrightarrow{\ \partial\ }H^{n+1}_c(X_h^\circ,\mathcal L)\to H^{n+1}_c(X_h,\mathcal L)\to0.
\]
Thus $\partial$ is injective. It is Frobenius-equivariant, and its source is a line on which Frobenius acts trivially (Lemma~\ref{lem:t0}). Hence its image is a Frobenius-stable line of weight $0$, which by Proposition~\ref{prop:weights-torus} is the unique such line in $H^{n+1}_c(X_h^\circ,\mathcal L)\cong H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathcal N_h)$. This proves (ii). For (iii), $H^{n+1}_c(X_h,\mathcal L)$ is the cokernel of $\partial$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:weights-torus}, the part of weight $\le n$ of $H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathcal N_h)$ is the image of $\mathcal N_h^{I_0}$, and its quotient is pure of weight $n+1$ and of dimension $r(n)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:frob-invariants}, $\operatorname{Frob}_q$ acts on $\mathcal N_h^{I_0}$ as $q^k$ on a subspace $E_k$ of dimension $m_{n,k}$, with $\mathcal N_h^{I_0}=\bigoplus_kE_k$, and the image of $\partial$ is the line $E_0$. Hence the part of weight $\le n$ of the cokernel is $\bigoplus_{k\ge1}E_k$, which proves (iii).

For (iv), the vanishing and the isomorphism follow from (i) and the first paragraph. The Grothendieck--Lefschetz trace formula on $Y_h$ gives $\Sigma_n(h)=\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{Tr}\big(\operatorname{Frob}_q\mid H^i_c(Y_h,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))\big)$, which reduces to the displayed formula. The Tate twist $(1)$ divides eigenvalues by $q$ and lowers weights by $2$, which gives the eigenvalues and~\eqref{eq:exact-formula}. Since an eigenvalue of weight $w$ has absolute value $q^{w/2}$, the bound on $\tau_q(h)$ follows.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:all-h}
Let $h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n$, and let $a$ be the number of nonzero coordinates of $h$. Then $H^i_c(Y_h\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))=0$ for $i\ne n-1$, $\dim H^{n-1}_c(Y_h\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))=2^a-1$, and $\Sigma_n(h)=(-1)^{n-1}\operatorname{Tr}\big(\operatorname{Frob}_q\mid H^{n-1}_c(Y_h,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))\big)$. For $a\ge2$ the eigenvalues are those of Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}(iv) with $n$ replaced by $a$; for $a=1$ and $h_i\ne0$ the single eigenvalue is $\psi_q(-h_i/\lambda)$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
If $a=0$, then $Y_h$ is empty, since $\lambda\ne0$. Otherwise let $I$ be the set of indices of the nonzero coordinates, $h_I$ the vector they form, and $f_I(u_I)=\sum_{i\in I}u_i^{-1}$. Then $Y_h\cong Y_{h_I}\times\mathbb{G}_m^{n-a}$, where $Y_{h_I}\subset\mathbb{G}_m^I$ is defined by $\langle h_I,u_I\rangle=-\lambda$, and $\mathcal{L}_\psi(f)\cong\mathcal{L}_\psi(f_I)\boxtimes\boxtimes_{i\notin I}\mathcal{L}_\psi(u_i^{-1})$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:t0} and the K\"unneth formula,
\[
R\Gamma_c\big(Y_h\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f)\big)\cong R\Gamma_c\big(Y_{h_I}\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f_I)\big)[-(n-a)],
\]
compatibly with $\operatorname{Frob}_q$. For $a\ge2$, Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre} applied to $h_I$ gives the assertions. For $a=1$, $Y_{h_I}$ is the point $u_i=-\lambda/h_i$, at which $\operatorname{Frob}_q$ acts on the stalk of $\mathcal{L}_\psi(u_i^{-1})$ by $\psi_q(-h_i/\lambda)$. The trace formula concludes.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:DL}
Let $T$ be an excellent noetherian scheme, $f\colon\mathbb P^1_T\to T$ the projection, $D\subset\mathbb P^1_T$ a closed subscheme finite and \'etale over $T$, $j\colon V=\mathbb P^1_T\smallsetminus D\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^1_T$ the inclusion, and $F$ a lisse sheaf of constant rank on $V$. Let $\sigma_F$ be the function $\bar t\mapsto\sum_{x\in D_{\bar t}}\operatorname{Swan}_x(F|_{V_{\bar t}})$ on geometric points of $T$.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item The function $\sigma_F$ is constructible.
\item If $\sigma_F$ is locally constant, then $R^if_*(j_!F)$ is lisse on $T$ for every $i$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:constant-rank}
Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre} shows that the stalks of $R^{n+1}\pi_!\mathcal L$ have the same dimension $2^n-1$ at all geometric points of $S$. This alone does not imply that the sheaf is lisse, even over a smooth connected base. For instance, on $\mathbb A^1$ the constructible sheaf $i_*\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell\oplus j_!\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$, where $i\colon\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1$ and $j\colon\mathbb{G}_m\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1$, has one-dimensional stalks everywhere but is not locally constant. This is why we use Theorem~\ref{thm:DL}.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:lisse}
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item Let $q_1\colon\mathbb{G}_m^n\times\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times S\to\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times S$ be the projection. Then $Rq_{1!}\mathcal L\cong\mathcal N[-n]$, where
\[
\mathcal N=\Big(\bigotimes_{i=1}^n[\times h_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}\Big)\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(\lambda t),\qquad[\times h_i](t,h)=h_it,
\]
is lisse of rank $2^n$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times S$.
\item $R^i\pi^\circ_!\mathcal L=0$ for $i\ne n+1$, and $\mathcal H_n$ is lisse of rank $2^n$.
\item $R^i\pi_!\mathcal L=0$ for $i\ne n+1$, and there is an exact sequence of lisse sheaves
\[
0\longrightarrow\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell\xrightarrow{\ \partial\ }\mathcal H_n\longrightarrow\mathcal G_n\longrightarrow0,
\]
in which $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$ is the constant sheaf, with trivial Frobenius action. In particular $\mathcal G_n$ is lisse of rank $2^n-1$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:integrate-t} its stalk at $h$ is $H^{n-1}_c(Y_h,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))(-1)$.
\item $\mathcal G_n$ has a unique increasing filtration $\mathrm W_\bullet$ by lisse subsheaves such that $\operatorname{gr}^{\mathrm W}_w\mathcal G_n$ is pointwise pure of weight $w$. The nonzero graded pieces are $\operatorname{gr}^{\mathrm W}_{2k}\mathcal G_n$, of rank $m_{n,k}$ for $1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, and $\mathcal W_n:=\operatorname{gr}^{\mathrm W}_{n+1}\mathcal G_n$, of rank $r(n)$. The inverse image $\mathcal H_n^{\le n}\subset\mathcal H_n$ of $\mathrm W_{\le n}\mathcal G_n$ is a lisse subsheaf, pointwise mixed of weights $\le n$, and $\mathcal H_n/\mathcal H_n^{\le n}\cong\mathcal W_n$.
\item For $h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)$ put $A_q(h)=\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_h\mid\mathcal W_n)$. Then
\[
(-1)^{n-1}q\,\Sigma_n(h)=A_q(h)+B_q(h),\qquad|A_q(h)|\le r(n)\,q^{(n+1)/2},\qquad B_q(h)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}m_{n,k}\,q^k.
\]
\item For $1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ there is an isomorphism $\operatorname{gr}^{\mathrm W}_{2k}\mathcal G_n\cong\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell(-k)^{\oplus m_{n,k}}$ of lisse sheaves on $S$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular Theorem~\ref{thmB} holds.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
(i) This is the relative form of Proposition~\ref{prop:fibration}(i). The same decomposition of $\mathcal L$, (K4), proper base change along $(t,h)\mapsto h_it$, the K\"unneth formula over $\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times S$ and the projection formula apply. Each $[\times h_i]^*\mathrm{Kl}$ is lisse of rank $2$, being the inverse image of $\mathrm{Kl}$ by a morphism to $\mathbb{G}_m$.

(ii) Let $\operatorname{pr}_S\colon\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times S\to S$ be the projection, and apply Theorem~\ref{thm:DL} with $T=S$, $D=\{0,\infty\}\times S$ and $F=\mathcal N$. At a geometric point $\bar h$ above a closed point of $S$, Proposition~\ref{prop:fibration}(ii) gives $\operatorname{Swan}_0(\mathcal N_{\bar h})=0$ and $\operatorname{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal N_{\bar h})=2^n$, so $\sigma_{\mathcal N}(\bar h)=2^n$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:DL}(i), every fibre of $\sigma_{\mathcal N}$ is a constructible subset of $S$. As $S$ is of finite type over $\mathbb{F}_p$, Hilbert's Nullstellensatz shows that every nonempty constructible subset of $S$ contains a closed point. Hence $\sigma_{\mathcal N}$ is constant, equal to $2^n$, and by Theorem~\ref{thm:DL}(ii) the sheaf $R^i\operatorname{pr}_{S!}\mathcal N$ is lisse for every $i$, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:fibration}(iii) it vanishes for $i\ne1$ and has rank $2^n$ for $i=1$. The Leray spectral sequence for $\pi^\circ=\operatorname{pr}_S\circ q_1$ and (i) give $R\pi^\circ_!\mathcal L\cong R\operatorname{pr}_{S!}\mathcal N[-n]$, whence (ii).

(iii) The excision triangle for the open subscheme $X^\circ$ and its closed complement $Z$ gives a long exact sequence
\[
\cdots\to R^i\pi^\circ_!\mathcal L\to R^i\pi_!\mathcal L\to R^i\pi_{Z!}(\mathcal L|_Z)\xrightarrow{\ \partial\ }R^{i+1}\pi^\circ_!\mathcal L\to\cdots.
\]
On $Z\cong\mathbb{G}_m^n\times S$ the phase is $\sum_iu_i^{-1}$, which does not involve $h$. So $R\pi_{Z!}(\mathcal L|_Z)$ is the constant complex with value $R\Gamma_c\big(\mathbb{G}_m^n\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\boxtimes_i\mathcal{L}_\psi(u_i^{-1})\big)$, which by Lemma~\ref{lem:t0} is $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell[-n]$ with trivial Frobenius action. Together with (ii), the sequence shows that $R^i\pi_!\mathcal L=0$ for $i\notin\{n,n+1\}$, and it reduces to an exact sequence
\[
0\to R^n\pi_!\mathcal L\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell\xrightarrow{\ \partial\ }\mathcal H_n\to\mathcal G_n\to0.
\]
Lisse sheaves on the connected normal scheme $S$ form an abelian subcategory of the constructible sheaves, equivalent to the category of continuous representations of $\pi_1(S)$; so $\ker\partial=R^n\pi_!\mathcal L$ and $\operatorname{coker}\partial=\mathcal G_n$ are lisse. By proper base change and Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}(ii), the map $\partial$ is injective on the stalk at a geometric point above a closed point of $S$. A lisse sheaf on the connected scheme $S$ with one zero stalk vanishes; hence $R^n\pi_!\mathcal L=0$, which proves (iii). The stalk of $\mathcal G_n$ at any geometric point $h$ is $H^{n+1}_c(X_h,\mathcal L)$ by proper base change, and this is $H^{n-1}_c(Y_h,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))(-1)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:integrate-t}.

(iv) The sheaf $\mathcal G_n$ is mixed by \cite[Th.~3.3.1]{Deligne}. Since $S$ is normal and connected, \cite[3.4.1]{Deligne} provides the unique filtration $\mathrm W_\bullet$ by lisse subsheaves with pointwise pure graded pieces. Let $h$ be a closed point of $S$, with residue field $\mathbb{F}_q$. The stalks at $\bar h$ of the subsheaves $\mathrm W_w\mathcal G_n$ form a $\operatorname{Frob}_h$-stable filtration of $(\mathcal G_n)_{\bar h}$ whose $w$-th graded piece is pure of weight $w$. Hence the rank of the lisse sheaf $\operatorname{gr}^{\mathrm W}_w\mathcal G_n$ is the number of eigenvalues of weight $w$, counted with multiplicity, of $\operatorname{Frob}_h$ on $(\mathcal G_n)_{\bar h}=H^{n+1}_c(X_h\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal L)$. These numbers are given by Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}(iii), a statement about the single fibre over $h$, proved in Section~\ref{sec:fibre} from Propositions~\ref{prop:fibration}, \ref{prop:weights-torus} and~\ref{prop:frob-invariants} and Lemma~\ref{lem:t0} alone. The assertions on $\mathcal H_n^{\le n}$ follow, as $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$ has weight $0\le n$.

(v) By Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}(iv), $\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_h\mid(\mathcal G_n)_h)=q\operatorname{Tr}\big(\operatorname{Frob}_q\mid H^{n-1}_c(Y_h,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f))\big)=(-1)^{n-1}q\Sigma_n(h)$. Decomposing the trace along $\mathrm W_\bullet$ gives $A_q(h)+B_q(h)$, where $B_q(h)$ is the sum of the traces on the $\operatorname{gr}^{\mathrm W}_{2k}\mathcal G_n$. The bound on $A_q(h)$ follows from the weight and the rank in (iv). By Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}(iii), $\operatorname{Frob}_h$ acts on the stalk of $\operatorname{gr}^{\mathrm W}_{2k}\mathcal G_n$ at $\bar h$ as multiplication by $q^k$, which gives the formula for $B_q(h)$.

(vi) Put $\mathcal E=\operatorname{gr}^{\mathrm W}_{2k}\mathcal G_n\otimes\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell(k)$, a lisse sheaf of rank $m=m_{n,k}$, pointwise pure of weight $0$. By the proof of~(v), $\operatorname{Frob}_h$ acts trivially on the stalk of $\mathcal E$ at $\bar h$, for every closed point $h$ of $S$. Hence $q^{-n}\sum_{h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)}\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_h\mid\mathcal E)=q^{-n}(q-1)^nm$, which tends to $m$ as $q\to\infty$ through powers of $p$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:averages}, applied with $T=S$ and $d=n$, the geometric fundamental group $\pi_1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ acts trivially on the geometric generic stalk of $\mathcal E$. So $\pi_1(S)$ acts on it through $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p/\mathbb{F}_p)$, which is topologically generated by the image of $\operatorname{Frob}_{h_0}$ for the rational point $h_0=(1,\dots,1)$, and $\operatorname{Frob}_{h_0}$ acts trivially. Hence $\mathcal E$ is constant, which is~(vi).
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:collision}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:crit}, the phase has $2^{n-1}$ critical points for $h\in\Omega_n$, but only $2^{n-1}-1$ at a point $h_0$ where exactly one pair $\{\pm\varepsilon_0\}$ satisfies $L_{\varepsilon_0}=0$. No two critical points collide there. Indeed, the critical locus of $F_n$ in $\mathbb{G}_m^n\times\mathbb{G}_m\times S$ is \'etale over $S$, because its relative Jacobian is the Hessian, which is invertible at every critical point for every $h$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:crit}). The drop in the number of points reflects a failure of finiteness. Instead, the critical point attached to $\{\pm\varepsilon_0\}$ escapes to infinity. As functions of the square roots $s_i$, its coordinates $u_i=-\lambda\varepsilon_{0,i}/(s_iL_{\varepsilon_0})$ have a pole and $t=L_{\varepsilon_0}^2/\lambda^2$ has a zero along $L_{\varepsilon_0}=0$. This is the degeneration of the phase on the face $\sigma^*$ of $P_n$ described in Remark~\ref{rem:AS}(b). Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse} shows that $\mathcal G_n$ is nevertheless lisse across these divisors; that is, $\mathcal G_n$ has no local monodromy along them. The proof never passes through the critical points: it only uses that the Swan conductors of $\mathcal N_h$ at $0$ and $\infty$ do not depend on $h$. This is consistent with Proposition~\ref{prop:nondeg}, by which $F_n$ is non-degenerate with respect to $\Delta_n$ for every $h$.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:conv-model}
Let $\mathcal N_c$ be the restriction of the sheaf $\mathcal N$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse}(i) to $\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times C_c$; thus $\mathcal N_c=[\times h_1]^*\mathrm{Kl}\otimes\operatorname{pr}_t^*\mathcal M_c$ with $[\times h_1](t,h_1)=h_1t$. Then $R\operatorname{pr}_{h_1!}\mathcal N_c\cong\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}[-1]$ and
\[
\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}[1]\cong\mathrm{Kl}[1]*_!\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1].
\]
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse}(i) and its proof, $R\operatorname{pr}_{S!}\mathcal N\cong R\pi^\circ_!\mathcal L[n]$, and by Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse}(ii) the complex $R\pi^\circ_!\mathcal L$ is $\mathcal H_n[-n-1]$; so $R\operatorname{pr}_{S!}\mathcal N\cong\mathcal H_n[-1]$. Restriction to $C_c$ by proper base change gives the first isomorphism. The morphism $\Phi\colon\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}\to\mathbb{G}_m\times\mathbb{G}_m$, $\Phi(t,h_1)=(h_1t,t^{-1})$, is an isomorphism with inverse $(x,y)\mapsto(y^{-1},xy)$; it satisfies $\mu\circ\Phi=\operatorname{pr}_{h_1}$ and $\Phi^*(\mathrm{Kl}\boxtimes\iota^*\mathcal M_c)=\mathcal N_c$. Hence $R\operatorname{pr}_{h_1!}\mathcal N_c\cong R\mu_!(\mathrm{Kl}\boxtimes\iota^*\mathcal M_c)$. Since $\mathrm{Kl}[1]\boxtimes\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1]=(\mathrm{Kl}\boxtimes\iota^*\mathcal M_c)[2]$, we obtain $\mathrm{Kl}[1]*_!\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1]\cong R\operatorname{pr}_{h_1!}\mathcal N_c[2]\cong\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}[1]$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:local-data}
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $\mathrm{Kl}$ is lisse on $\mathbb{G}_m$ and pure of weight $1$. It is tame at $0$, with $\mathrm{Kl}(0)\cong\mathrm{U}(2)$, and totally wild at $\infty$, with $\operatorname{Swan}_\infty(\mathrm{Kl})=1$.
\item $\iota^*\mathcal M_c$ is lisse on $\mathbb{G}_m$ and pure of weight $n-1$. It is totally wild at $0$, with all breaks equal to $1$ and $\operatorname{Swan}_0=2^{n-1}$, and tame at $\infty$, with $(\iota^*\mathcal M_c)(\infty)\cong\mathrm{U}(2)^{\otimes(n-1)}$.
\item Neither $\mathrm{Kl}$ nor $\iota^*\mathcal M_c$ has, geometrically, a Kummer sheaf as a subsheaf, quotient sheaf or Jordan--H\"older constituent. Consequently $\mathrm{Kl}[1]$ and $\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1]$ have no Kummer subobject, quotient or constituent in the category of perverse sheaves.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
(i) is (K1)--(K3). For (ii), $\mathcal M_c$ is pure of weight $n-1$ by (K1). At $0$ it is tame with local monodromy $\mathrm{U}(2)^{\otimes(n-1)}$, and at $\infty$ all its breaks equal $1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:breaks}, exactly as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:fibration}(ii). The inversion $\iota$ exchanges $0$ and $\infty$, preserves purity, and carries the local monodromy of $\mathcal M_c$ at one point to that of $\iota^*\mathcal M_c$ at the other. It maps a topological generator of tame inertia to the inverse of one, and a unipotent automorphism and its inverse have the same Jordan blocks.

(iii) A Kummer sheaf is tame at $0$ and at $\infty$. Let $F$ be $\mathrm{Kl}$ or $\iota^*\mathcal M_c$, and let $x$ be a point at which $F$ is totally wild: $x=\infty$ for $\mathrm{Kl}$ and $x=0$ for $\iota^*\mathcal M_c$. Since $I^{\mathrm{w}}_x$ acts semisimply, no nonzero subquotient of $F(x)$ has nonzero $I^{\mathrm{w}}_x$-invariants. Hence no nonzero subquotient of $F$, in particular no Kummer sheaf, is tame at $x$. For the perverse statement, let $G$ run over the Jordan--H\"older constituents of $F$. By (P1) and induction on the length of $F$, the perverse sheaf $F[1]$ is a successive extension of the $G[1]$. Each $G[1]$ is simple, being the intermediate extension of an irreducible lisse sheaf placed in degree $-1$ \cite{BBD}. So the Jordan--H\"older constituents of $F[1]$ are the $G[1]$, and by (P1) none of them is of the form $\mathcal L_\chi[1]$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:tame}
The sheaves $\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}$, $\mathcal G_n|_{C_c}$ and $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}$ are tamely ramified at $h_1=0$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
\emph{Reduction.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse}(iii),(iv), there is an exact sequence $0\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell\to\mathcal H_n\to\mathcal G_n\to0$ with constant first term, and $\mathcal W_n$ is a quotient of $\mathcal G_n$. Since $I^{\mathrm{w}}_0$ acts semisimply, a representation on which it acts trivially on a subrepresentation and on the quotient is trivial, and trivial actions pass to subquotients. It therefore suffices to show that $\mathcal G_n|_{C_c}$ is tame at $h_1=0$.

\emph{A Fourier model.} Write $u'=(u_2,\dots,u_n)$, $f'(u')=\sum_{i\ge2}u_i^{-1}$, $B(u')=-\lambda-\sum_{i\ge2}c_iu_i$, $U=\{u'\in\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}:B(u')\ne0\}$ and $b=B^{-1}\colon U\to\mathbb{G}_{m,v}$. Let
\[
\mathcal Y=\Big\{(h_1,u)\in\mathbb{G}_m\times\mathbb{G}_m^n:\ h_1u_1+\sum_{i\ge2}c_iu_i=-\lambda\Big\},
\]
with projection $\pi_{\mathcal Y}$ to $\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:integrate-t} in its relative form over $C_c$, Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse}(iii) and proper base change,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:G-on-line}
R\pi_{\mathcal Y!}\mathcal{L}_\psi(f)\cong\mathcal G_n|_{C_c}(1)[-(n-1)].
\end{equation}
The map $(h_1,u)\mapsto(h_1,u')$ is an isomorphism $\mathcal Y\to\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}\times U$, with inverse given by $u_1=B(u')/h_1$, and it carries $f$ to $h_1b(u')+f'(u')$. Put $\mathcal R=Rb_!\mathcal{L}_\psi(f')$ on $\mathbb{G}_{m,v}$, let $j_v\colon\mathbb{G}_{m,v}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_v$ be the inclusion, and let
\[
\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K)=R\operatorname{pr}_{2!}\big(\operatorname{pr}_1^*K\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(vh_1)\big)[1]
\]
be the Fourier transform on $\mathbb A^1_v\times\mathbb A^1_{h_1}$, in Laumon's normalization \cite[(1.2.1.1)]{Laumon}. The projection formula and proper base change for $b\times\mathrm{id}$ give $R\pi_{\mathcal Y!}\mathcal{L}_\psi(f)\cong\operatorname{FT}_\psi(j_{v!}\mathcal R)[-1]|_{\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}}$. Therefore, by \eqref{eq:G-on-line},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:FT-model}
\operatorname{FT}_\psi(j_{v!}\mathcal R)|_{\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}}\cong\mathcal G_n|_{C_c}(1)[2-n].
\end{equation}

\emph{The complex $\mathcal R$ near $v=\infty$.} Let $w=v^{-1}$, and let $D_w=\mathbb A^1_w\smallsetminus\{-\lambda\}$, a neighbourhood of $w=0$. On $D_w$ the map $a(w)=\big(\lambda c_i/(\lambda+w)\big)_{i\ge2}$ is a morphism $D_w\to\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}$ with $a(0)=c$. In the coordinate $w$, the fibre of $b$ over $v=w^{-1}$ is $\{u'\in\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}:\sum_{i\ge2}c_iu_i=-(\lambda+w)\}$. The scheme $\{(w,u'):w\in D_w,\ \sum_{i\ge2}c_iu_i=-(\lambda+w)\}$ is the inverse image under $a$ of the universal family
\[
\mathcal Y_{n-1}=\{(h',u')\in\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}\times\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}:\langle h',u'\rangle=-\lambda\},
\]
because $\sum_i\lambda c_i(\lambda+w)^{-1}u_i=-\lambda$ is the same equation; the phase is $f'$ on both. Suppose first $n\ge3$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:integrate-t} and Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse}(iii) for $n-1\ge2$ variables, the direct image of $\mathcal{L}_\psi(f')$ along $\mathcal Y_{n-1}\to\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}$ is $\mathcal G_{n-1}(1)[-(n-2)]$, a lisse sheaf placed in one degree. By proper base change along $a$, the restriction of $\mathcal R$ to the punctured neighbourhood $D_w\smallsetminus\{0\}$ of $v=\infty$ is the restriction of the lisse sheaf $a^*\mathcal G_{n-1}(1)$ on $D_w$, placed in degree $n-2$. If $n=2$, the fibre is the single point $u_2=-(\lambda+w)/c_2$, and the restriction of $\mathcal R$ to $D_w\smallsetminus\{0\}$ is that of $\mathcal{L}_\psi(-c_2/(\lambda+w))$, which is lisse on $D_w$. In both cases $\mathcal R$ is, near $v=\infty$, a lisse sheaf in a single degree on which $I_\infty$ acts trivially.

\emph{Laumon's local Fourier transform.} We use three facts from \cite{Laumon}, valid for every perverse sheaf $P$ on $\mathbb A^1_v$. First, $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P)$ is perverse \cite[(1.3.2.3)]{Laumon}. Second, the vanishing cycles of $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P)$ at $h_1=0$ depend, as a representation of $I_0$, only on the representation $V$ of $I_\infty$ on $\mathcal H^{-1}(P)_{\bar\eta_\infty}$: there is an isomorphism of $I_0$-modules
\[
R^{-1}\Phi_0\big(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P)\big)\cong\mathcal F^{(\infty,0')}(V),
\]
where $\mathcal F^{(\infty,0')}$ is Laumon's local Fourier transform \cite[Prop.~(2.3.2.1)(iii) and D\'ef.~(2.4.2.3)]{Laumon}. Third, if all slopes of $V$ are $<1$, then $\operatorname{Swan}\big(\mathcal F^{(\infty,0')}(V)\big)=\operatorname{Swan}(V)$ \cite[Th.~(2.4.3)(ii)(b)]{Laumon}. Shifts and Tate twists do not change the action of inertia, so the normalization of $\operatorname{FT}_\psi$ plays no further role. Now let $P_i={}^p\mathcal H^i(j_{v!}\mathcal R)$ be the perverse cohomology sheaves, so that $j_{v!}\mathcal R$ is a successive extension of the $P_i[-i]$. By the previous step, the $I_\infty$-module $V_i=\mathcal H^{-1}(P_i)_{\bar\eta_\infty}$ is trivial for every $i$. In particular it has slope $0$, so $\operatorname{Swan}\big(\mathcal F^{(\infty,0')}(V_i)\big)=\operatorname{Swan}(V_i)=0$, and $I^{\mathrm{w}}_0$ acts trivially on the vanishing cycles $R^{-1}\Phi_0\big(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P_i)\big)$. On a small punctured neighbourhood of $0$, the perverse sheaf $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P_i)$ is a lisse sheaf placed in degree $-1$; let $\mathcal V_i$ be its generic stalk, an $I_0$-module. The triangle formed by the stalk at $0$, the nearby cycles and the vanishing cycles gives an exact sequence of $I_0$-modules
\[
\mathcal H^{-1}\big(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P_i)\big)_0\longrightarrow\mathcal V_i\longrightarrow R^{-1}\Phi_0\big(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P_i)\big),
\]
in which $I_0$ acts trivially on the image of the first arrow. As $I^{\mathrm{w}}_0$ acts semisimply on $\mathcal V_i$, and trivially both on the image of the first arrow and on the third term, it acts trivially on $\mathcal V_i$. Thus every $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P_i)$ is tame at $0$. Since $\operatorname{FT}_\psi$ is a triangulated functor, $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(j_{v!}\mathcal R)$ is a successive extension of the $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P_i)[-i]$. On a small punctured neighbourhood of $0$ all cohomology sheaves involved are lisse, so the long exact cohomology sequences and the semisimplicity of $I^{\mathrm{w}}_0$-actions show that every cohomology sheaf of $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(j_{v!}\mathcal R)$ is tame at $0$. By \eqref{eq:FT-model}, $\mathcal G_n|_{C_c}$ is tame at $h_1=0$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:jordan-poly}
Let $\mathcal A$ be a perverse sheaf on $\mathbb{G}_m\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$, let $F$ be a lisse sheaf on a dense open subset $U\subseteq\mathbb{G}_m$ with $\mathcal A|_U\cong F[1]$, and let $\chi$ be a character of finite order prime to $p$. For $x\in\{0,\infty\}$ and $i\ge1$, let $b^x_i(\mathcal A,\chi)$ be the number of Jordan blocks of size $i$ in the unipotent part of $(\mathcal L_\chi\otimes F)(x)$. Define $\mathsf P_{\mathcal A,\chi}\in\mathbb Z[T,T^{-1}]$ by
\[
\mathsf P_{\mathcal A,\chi}(T)=a_0(\mathcal A,\chi)+\sum_{i\ge1}\big(b^0_i(\mathcal A,\chi)\,T^{-i}+b^\infty_i(\mathcal A,\chi)\,T^{i}\big),
\]
where $a_0(\mathcal A,\chi)$ is chosen so that $\mathsf P_{\mathcal A,\chi}(1)=\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_m\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mathcal A)$. This Euler characteristic does not change if $\mathcal A$ is replaced by $\mathcal L_\chi\otimes\mathcal A$, since a tame twist preserves all local invariants.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:weight-dictionary}
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb{G}_m$ be a dense open subset over a finite field, and let $F_U$ be a lisse sheaf on $U$, pure of weight $-1$, without geometrically trivial subsheaf or quotient sheaf. Let $F$ be the direct image of $F_U$ on $\mathbb{G}_m$, let $j_\infty\colon\mathbb{G}_m\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^1\smallsetminus\{0\}$ and $j_0\colon\mathbb P^1\smallsetminus\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^1$ be the inclusions, and put
\[
\omega(F[1])=H^0\big(\mathbb P^1\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\,j_{0!}Rj_{\infty*}F[1]\big).
\]
Then $\dim\omega(F[1])=\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_m\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,F[1])$. For $i\ge1$, the number of Frobenius eigenvalues of weight $-i$ on $\omega(F[1])$ is $b^0_i(F[1],\mathbf 1)$ and the number of weight $+i$ is $b^\infty_i(F[1],\mathbf 1)$; all other eigenvalues have weight $0$. Equivalently, $\sum_w\big(\text{number of eigenvalues of weight }w\big)\,T^w=\mathsf P_{F[1],\mathbf 1}(T)$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Put $A=\mathbb P^1\smallsetminus\{0\}$, so that $\omega(F[1])=H^1_c\big(A\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,Rj_{\infty*}F\big)$. The complex $Rj_{\infty*}F$ has $j_{\infty*}F$ in degree $0$ and, in degree $1$, the skyscraper at $\infty$ with value $H^1(I_\infty,F(\infty))=F(\infty)_{I_\infty}(-1)$. The triangle $j_{\infty!}F\to Rj_{\infty*}F\to i_{\infty*}(Rj_{\infty*}F)_\infty$ gives an exact sequence
\[
\begin{aligned}
0&\to H^0_c(\mathbb{G}_m,F)\to H^0_c(A,Rj_{\infty*}F)\to F(\infty)^{I_\infty}\to H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_m,F)\\
&\to H^1_c(A,Rj_{\infty*}F)\to F(\infty)_{I_\infty}(-1)\to H^2_c(\mathbb{G}_m,F).
\end{aligned}
\]
The groups $H^0_c(\mathbb{G}_m,F)$ and $H^0_c(A,Rj_{\infty*}F)$ vanish, since $F$ has no nonzero sections supported at points and $A$ is affine. The group $H^2_c(\mathbb{G}_m,F)$, the geometric coinvariants of $F_U$ twisted by $(-1)$, vanishes by hypothesis. Next, there is an exact sequence
\[
0\to F(0)^{I_0}\oplus F(\infty)^{I_\infty}\to H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_m,F)\to H^1(\mathbb P^1,j_*F)\to0,
\]
obtained as in Proposition~\ref{prop:weights-torus} using $H^0(\mathbb{G}_m,F)=0$, whose right-hand term is pure of weight $0$ by \cite[3.2.3]{Deligne}. Combining the two sequences, $\omega(F[1])$ has a filtration with graded pieces $F(0)^{I_0}$, $H^1(\mathbb P^1,j_*F)$ and $F(\infty)_{I_\infty}(-1)$. In particular its dimension is $\dim H^1_c(\mathbb{G}_m,F)=\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_m,F[1])$. Invariants and coinvariants of $I_x$ come only from the unipotent part of $F(x)$. By \cite[1.8.4]{Deligne}, a Jordan block of size $i$ in the unipotent part of $F(0)$ contributes to $F(0)^{I_0}$ one eigenvalue of weight $-1-(i-1)=-i$. A block of size $i$ in the unipotent part of $F(\infty)$ contributes to $F(\infty)_{I_\infty}$ one eigenvalue of weight $-1+(i-1)$, hence to $F(\infty)_{I_\infty}(-1)$ one eigenvalue of weight $i$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:RL}
Let $k$ be a finite field of characteristic $p$, and let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ be pure perverse sheaves on $\mathbb{G}_m$ over $k$. Suppose that each of them is the middle extension of a lisse sheaf on a dense open subset, placed in degree $-1$, and that neither has, over $\bar k$, a subobject or quotient of the form $\mathcal L_\rho[1]$. Suppose moreover that $\mathcal A*_{\mathrm{mid}}\mathcal B$ has, over $\bar k$, no nonzero punctual subobject or quotient. Then for every character $\chi$ of finite order prime to $p$,
\[
\mathsf P_{\mathcal A*_{\mathrm{mid}}\mathcal B,\chi}=\mathsf P_{\mathcal A,\chi}\cdot\mathsf P_{\mathcal B,\chi}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
A product formula of this kind was proved by Rojas-Le\'on \cite[Prop.~6.1]{RojasLeon-conv} with his local convolution functors. We give a proof based on Deligne's fibre functor, which also fixes the normalization.

\emph{Reductions.} Both sides depend only on $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ over $\bar k$, and the formation of $\mathcal A*_{\mathrm{mid}}\mathcal B$ commutes with extension of scalars (\S\ref{sec:conv}). The hypotheses are preserved by finite extensions of $k$: purity is, the formation of $j_*$ commutes with \'etale base change, and the remaining conditions are geometric. If $\chi$ has order $m$, we may therefore assume that $\mu_m\subset k$. Then $\chi$ is the Kummer character attached to a character of $k^\times$, again denoted $\chi$, and $\mathcal L_\chi$ is a lisse sheaf of rank one on $\mathbb{G}_m$ over $k$, pure of weight $0$. Next, for $\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell^\times$ let $\alpha^{\deg}$ be the geometrically constant sheaf of rank one on which $\operatorname{Frob}_k$ acts by $\alpha$.
