The projection formula gives $(\mathcal A\otimes\alpha^{\deg})*_{\mathrm{mid}}(\mathcal B\otimes\beta^{\deg})\cong(\mathcal A*_{\mathrm{mid}}\mathcal B)\otimes(\alpha\beta)^{\deg}$, and these twists change neither side of the formula, because the polynomials $\mathsf P$ are geometric. Choosing $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of suitable absolute values, we may assume that $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ are pure of weight $0$.

\emph{The fibre functor.} Over $\bar k$, $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ lie in Katz's class $\mathcal P$ (\S\ref{sec:conv}); that is, they are objects of the category $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{arith}}$ of \cite[Ch.~4]{Katz-Conv}. The objects of $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{arith}}$ that are pure of weight $0$ are stable under middle convolution \cite[Ch.~4, paragraph after Th.~4.1]{Katz-Conv}. So $\mathcal K=\mathcal A*_{\mathrm{mid}}\mathcal B$ lies in $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{arith}}$ and is pure of weight $0$; in particular, over $\bar k$ it has no subobject or quotient of the form $\mathcal L_\rho[1]$. Let $j'\colon\mathbb{G}_m\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1$ be the inclusion, and for a perverse sheaf $\mathcal N$ on $\mathbb{G}_m$ over $k$ put
\[
\omega_\chi(\mathcal N)=H^0\big(\mathbb A^1\otimes\bar k,\,j'_!(\mathcal L_\chi\otimes\mathcal N)\big),
\]
on which $\operatorname{Frob}_k$ acts. By \cite[Th.~3.1 and Cor.~3.2]{Katz-Conv}, $\omega_\chi$ is a fibre functor, for middle convolution, on Katz's Tannakian category $\mathcal P$. By \cite[beginning of Ch.~5]{Katz-Conv}, for every character $\chi$ of $k^\times$ the action of $\operatorname{Frob}_k$ on $\omega_\chi$ is an element of the Tannakian group of the category generated by $\mathcal A\oplus\mathcal B$ in $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{arith}}$, that is, an automorphism of the fibre functor compatible with its tensor structure. (The tensor isomorphisms of $\omega_\chi$ are canonical, so they commute with transport of structure by $\mathrm{Gal}(\bar k/k)$, that is, with the action of $\operatorname{Frob}_k$, for every $\chi$. Katz's further condition that $\chi$ be good for $\mathcal A\oplus\mathcal B$ serves to make the eigenvalues unitary, which we do not need: the weights are computed below.) In particular there is an isomorphism $\omega_\chi(\mathcal K)\cong\omega_\chi(\mathcal A)\otimes\omega_\chi(\mathcal B)$ compatible with $\operatorname{Frob}_k$.

\emph{Weights.} Let $\mathcal N$ be one of $\mathcal A$, $\mathcal B$, $\mathcal K$, and put $\mathcal N'=\mathcal L_\chi\otimes\mathcal N$, a perverse sheaf pure of weight $0$. Over $\bar k$, $\mathcal N'$ has no subobject or quotient isomorphic to $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell[1]$, because $\mathcal N$ has none isomorphic to $\mathcal L_{\chi^{-1}}[1]$. Next, there are a dense open subset $U\subseteq\mathbb{G}_m$, with inclusion $j\colon U\hookrightarrow\mathbb{G}_m$, and a lisse sheaf $G_U$ on $U$ with $\mathcal N'\cong(j_*G_U)[1]$. For $\mathcal N=\mathcal A$ or $\mathcal B$ this holds by hypothesis, with $G_U=\mathcal L_\chi|_U\otimes F_U$ if $\mathcal N=(j_*F_U)[1]$, because tensoring with the lisse sheaf $\mathcal L_\chi$ commutes with $j_*$. For $\mathcal N=\mathcal K$, the hypothesis on $\mathcal A*_{\mathrm{mid}}\mathcal B$ shows that $\mathcal N'=\mathcal L_\chi\otimes\mathcal K$ has no nonzero punctual subobject or quotient over $\bar k$, hence none over $k$, since extension of scalars is exact and faithful. By (P2), $\mathcal N'$ is of the form $G_U[1]$ on some dense open subset $U$, and (P4)(a) gives $\mathcal N'\cong(j_*G_U)[1]$. On $U$ we have $\mathcal N'=G_U[1]$ and $D(G_U[1])=G_U^\vee(1)[1]$, so purity of $\mathcal N'$ of weight $0$ means that $G_U$ is pointwise pure of weight $-1$. By (P4)(b), applied over $\bar k$ with $L=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$, the sheaf $G_U$ has no geometrically trivial subsheaf or quotient sheaf. Thus Lemma~\ref{lem:weight-dictionary} applies to $G_U$. By the remark following that lemma, its functor $\omega$ satisfies $\omega(\mathcal N')=\omega_\chi(\mathcal N)$, and $\mathsf P_{\mathcal N',\mathbf 1}=\mathsf P_{\mathcal N,\chi}$ by Definition~\ref{def:jordan-poly}. Hence
\[
\mathsf P_{\mathcal N,\chi}(T)=\sum_w\big(\text{number of eigenvalues of }\operatorname{Frob}_k\text{ on }\omega_\chi(\mathcal N)\text{ of weight }w\big)\,T^w .
\]
The eigenvalues of $\operatorname{Frob}_k$ on $\omega_\chi(\mathcal A)\otimes\omega_\chi(\mathcal B)$ are the products of those on the two factors, counted with multiplicity, and weights add. So the right-hand side is multiplicative in tensor products, and the isomorphism $\omega_\chi(\mathcal K)\cong\omega_\chi(\mathcal A)\otimes\omega_\chi(\mathcal B)$ gives the theorem.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:binomial}
For every $n\ge2$, $2r(n-1)+\kappa_1=r(n)$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Since $r(m)=2^m-\binom m{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}$, the claim is that $2\binom{n-1}{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}-\kappa_1=\binom n{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$. If $n=2m$, then $\kappa_1=0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:CG}, and $\binom{2m}m=\binom{2m-1}{m-1}+\binom{2m-1}m=2\binom{2m-1}{m-1}$. If $n=2m+1$, then $\kappa_1=\binom{2m}m-\binom{2m}{m-1}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:CG}, and $2\binom{2m}m-\kappa_1=\binom{2m}m+\binom{2m}{m-1}=\binom{2m+1}m$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:boundary}
Let $\mathcal K=\mathrm{Kl}[1]*_{\mathrm{mid}}\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1]$.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}[1]\cong\mathcal K$.
\item $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}$ is tame at $h_1=0$, and its local monodromy there is unipotent, with $r(n-1)$ Jordan blocks of size $2$, $\kappa_1$ blocks of size $1$, and no block of size $\ge3$.
\item The tame part of $(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})(\infty)$ is unipotent, with $\kappa_j$ Jordan blocks of size $j-2$ for each $j\ge3$, and $\operatorname{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})=2^{n-1}$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular Theorem~\ref{thmC}(i) and~(iv) hold, as well as the assertions of Theorem~\ref{thmC}(ii) on the tame part and on the Swan conductor.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
We work with perverse sheaves on $C_c$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Lemma~\ref{lem:conv-model} and the definition of $*_{\mathrm{mid}}$ give morphisms
\[
\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}[1]\cong\mathrm{Kl}[1]*_!\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1]\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal K\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Kl}[1]*_*\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1].
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse}(iv) and (P1), there is also an epimorphism $\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}[1]\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}[1]$ with kernel $\mathcal H_n^{\le n}|_{C_c}[1]$. Step~0 shows that $\mathcal K$ has no nonzero punctual subobject or quotient, and Steps~1 and~2 compute the local monodromy of $\mathcal K$. Step~3 shows that $\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}[1]\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal K$ factors through $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}[1]$, and Step~4 that the resulting epimorphism $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}[1]\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal K$ is an isomorphism.

\emph{Step 0: no punctual subobject or quotient.} We argue over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$, using that the formation of $\mathcal K$ commutes with extension of scalars (\S\ref{sec:conv}). The sheaf $\mathcal H_n$ is lisse, so by (P3) the perverse sheaf $\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}[1]$ has no nonzero punctual quotient; hence neither has its quotient $\mathcal K$. For subobjects, since $\mathcal K\subseteq\mathrm{Kl}[1]*_*\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1]$, by (P3) it suffices to show that $\operatorname{Hom}(\delta_x,\mathrm{Kl}[1]*_*\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1])=0$ for every closed point $x$ of $\mathbb{G}_m\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$. Adjunction gives
\[
\operatorname{Hom}\big(\delta_x,R\mu_*(\mathrm{Kl}\boxtimes\iota^*\mathcal M_c)[2]\big)\cong H^0\big(\mu^{-1}(x),(\mathrm{Kl}\boxtimes\iota^*\mathcal M_c)|_{\mu^{-1}(x)}\big)(-1).
\]
This vanishes, because $\mu^{-1}(x)\cong\mathbb{G}_m$ and the restricted sheaf $y\mapsto\mathrm{Kl}(y)\otimes\mathcal M_c(y/x)$ is totally wild at $y=\infty$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:breaks}. Thus $\mathcal K$ has no nonzero punctual subobject or quotient over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$. Moreover $\mathrm{Kl}[1]$ and $\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1]$ are lisse sheaves on $\mathbb{G}_m$ placed in degree $-1$, pure as perverse sheaves by Lemma~\ref{lem:local-data}(i),(ii), and by Lemma~\ref{lem:local-data}(iii) neither has a subobject or quotient of the form $\mathcal L_\rho[1]$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$. So the pair $\mathrm{Kl}[1]$, $\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1]$ satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:RL}.

\emph{Step 1: the two polynomials.} Take first $\chi=\mathbf 1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:local-data}(i), $b^0_2(\mathrm{Kl}[1],\mathbf 1)=1$ and all other $b$ vanish, while $\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathrm{Kl}[1])=\operatorname{Swan}_\infty(\mathrm{Kl})=1$; so $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{Kl}[1],\mathbf 1}=T^{-2}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:local-data}(ii), $b^\infty_j(\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1],\mathbf 1)=\kappa_j$ and $b^0_j(\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1],\mathbf 1)=0$, while $\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1])=\operatorname{Swan}_0(\iota^*\mathcal M_c)=2^{n-1}$. Since $2^{n-1}-\sum_j\kappa_j=2^{n-1}-\binom{n-1}{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}=r(n-1)$, this gives
\[
\mathsf P_{\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1],\mathbf 1}(T)=r(n-1)+\sum_{j\ge1}\kappa_jT^j.
\]
For $\chi\ne\mathbf 1$, twisting by $\mathcal L_\chi$ kills the unipotent parts at both points and does not change Swan conductors. Hence $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{Kl}[1],\chi}=1$ and $\mathsf P_{\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1],\chi}=2^{n-1}$.

\emph{Step 2: the product.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:RL},
\[
\mathsf P_{\mathcal K,\mathbf 1}(T)=r(n-1)\,T^{-2}+\kappa_1T^{-1}+\kappa_2+\sum_{j\ge3}\kappa_jT^{j-2},\qquad\mathsf P_{\mathcal K,\chi}=2^{n-1}\quad(\chi\ne\mathbf 1).
\]
Let $F_{\mathcal K}$ be the lisse sheaf on a dense open subset of $\mathbb{G}_m$ with $\mathcal K\cong F_{\mathcal K}[1]$ there. Let $x\in\{0,\infty\}$, and write the tame part of $F_{\mathcal K}(x)$ as $\bigoplus_\rho\mathcal L_\rho\otimes U_\rho$ (\S\ref{sec:conventions}). Every character $\rho\ne\mathbf 1$ of finite order prime to $p$ of the tame inertia at $x$ is the local monodromy at $x$ of a Kummer sheaf $\mathcal L_{\chi^{-1}}$ with $\chi\ne\mathbf 1$. The unipotent part of $(\mathcal L_\chi\otimes F_{\mathcal K})(x)$ is then $U_\rho$. Since $\mathsf P_{\mathcal K,\chi}$ is constant, all $b^x_i(\mathcal K,\chi)$ vanish, so $U_\rho=0$. Hence the tame parts of $F_{\mathcal K}(0)$ and $F_{\mathcal K}(\infty)$ are unipotent. By Definition~\ref{def:jordan-poly}, for $i\ge1$ the coefficient of $T^{-i}$ in $\mathsf P_{\mathcal K,\mathbf 1}$ is $b^0_i(\mathcal K,\mathbf 1)$ and that of $T^i$ is $b^\infty_i(\mathcal K,\mathbf 1)$. Comparing with the display:
\begin{itemize}
\item $b^0_2(\mathcal K,\mathbf 1)=r(n-1)$, $b^0_1(\mathcal K,\mathbf 1)=\kappa_1$, and $b^0_i(\mathcal K,\mathbf 1)=0$ for $i\ge3$;
\item $b^\infty_i(\mathcal K,\mathbf 1)=\kappa_{i+2}$ for $i\ge1$;
\item the constant term $\kappa_2$ is $a_0(\mathcal K,\mathbf 1)$.
\end{itemize}
Thus the tame part of $F_{\mathcal K}(0)$ consists of $r(n-1)$ Jordan blocks of size $2$, $\kappa_1$ blocks of size $1$ and no others, and that of $F_{\mathcal K}(\infty)$ of $\kappa_j$ blocks of size $j-2$ for each $j\ge3$ and no others. Finally $\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathcal K)=\mathsf P_{\mathcal K,\mathbf 1}(1)=2^{n-1}$.

\emph{Step 3: $\mathcal K$ is a quotient of $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}[1]$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:conv-model}, $\mathcal K$ is a quotient of $\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}[1]$ in the category of perverse sheaves. We first determine the weights of $\mathcal K$ on a dense open subset. Put $\mathcal L_c=\mathrm{Kl}\boxtimes\iota^*\mathcal M_c$, a lisse sheaf on $\mathbb{G}_m^2$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, pure of weight $n$, so that $\mathrm{Kl}[1]*_!\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1]=R\mu_!\mathcal L_c[2]$ and $\mathrm{Kl}[1]*_*\iota^*\mathcal M_c[1]=R\mu_*\mathcal L_c[2]$. Let $U\subseteq C_c$ be a dense open subset, defined over $\mathbb{F}_q$, on which these two perverse sheaves and $\mathcal K$ are of the form $A[1]$, $B[1]$ and $F_{\mathcal K}[1]$, with $A$, $B$ and $F_{\mathcal K}$ lisse. By (P1), on $U$ the epimorphism $A[1]\to F_{\mathcal K}[1]$ and the monomorphism $F_{\mathcal K}[1]\to B[1]$ come from a surjection $A\to F_{\mathcal K}$ and an injection $F_{\mathcal K}\to B$ of lisse sheaves. The sheaf $A=R^1\mu_!\mathcal L_c|_U$ is pointwise mixed of weights $\le n+1$ by \cite[Th.~3.3.1]{Deligne}. By Verdier duality, $D(R\mu_*\mathcal L_c[2])\cong R\mu_!\big(\mathcal L_c^\vee(2)[2]\big)$; restricting to $U$ gives $B^\vee(1)\cong R^1\mu_!(\mathcal L_c^\vee)(2)|_U$, which is pointwise mixed of weights $\le-n-3$, again by \cite[Th.~3.3.1]{Deligne}. So $B$ is pointwise mixed of weights $\ge n+1$. As $F_{\mathcal K}$ is a quotient of $A$ and a subsheaf of $B$, it is pointwise pure of weight $n+1$. Now consider the composite
\[
\phi\colon\mathcal H_n^{\le n}|_{C_c}[1]\longrightarrow\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}[1]\longrightarrow\mathcal K.
\]
It is a morphism of perverse sheaves on $C_c$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$: the inclusion $\mathcal H_n^{\le n}\subset\mathcal H_n$ is defined over $\mathbb{F}_p$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse}(iv)), the isomorphism of Lemma~\ref{lem:conv-model} is defined over $\mathbb{F}_q$, and so is the natural morphism $R\mu_!\to R\mu_*$ whose image is $\mathcal K$. Let $U$ be as above. As $\mathcal H_n^{\le n}$ is lisse, $\phi|_U=\phi_0[1]$ for a morphism of lisse sheaves $\phi_0\colon\mathcal H_n^{\le n}|_U\to F_{\mathcal K}$. Let $x\in U$ be a closed point and $\bar x$ a geometric point above it. The stalk map $\phi_{0,\bar x}$ commutes with $\operatorname{Frob}_x$, so it maps the generalized eigenspace of $\operatorname{Frob}_x$ for an eigenvalue $\alpha$ into the generalized eigenspace for $\alpha$, because $(\operatorname{Frob}_x-\alpha)^N\phi_{0,\bar x}=\phi_{0,\bar x}(\operatorname{Frob}_x-\alpha)^N$ for all $N$. Every eigenvalue on the source has weight $\le n$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse}(iv)), and every eigenvalue on the target has weight $n+1$. The two spectra are disjoint, so $\phi_{0,\bar x}=0$. Lisse sheaves on the connected scheme $U$ correspond to continuous representations of $\pi_1(U,\bar x)$ through their stalks at $\bar x$, and a morphism of lisse sheaves is determined by its stalk at $\bar x$. Hence $\phi_0=0$, that is, $\phi|_U=0$. Restriction to $U$ is exact on perverse sheaves (P2), so the image of $\phi$ is a perverse subobject of $\mathcal K$ whose restriction to $U$ vanishes, that is, a perverse sheaf supported on the finite set $C_c\smallsetminus U$. But $\mathcal K$ has no nonzero punctual subobject over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ (Step~0), hence none over $\mathbb{F}_q$, since extension of scalars is exact and faithful. Hence the composite is zero, and $\mathcal K$ is a quotient of $\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}[1]/\mathcal H_n^{\le n}|_{C_c}[1]\cong\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}[1]$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse}(iv)).

\emph{Step 4: comparison of ranks.} Let $\mathcal N$ be the kernel of the epimorphism $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}[1]\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal K$ of Step~3. With $U$ as in Step~3, this epimorphism restricts on $U$ to $f[1]$ for a surjection $f\colon\mathcal W_n|_U\to F_{\mathcal K}$ of lisse sheaves, by (P1). By Proposition~\ref{prop:tame}, $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}$ is tame at $h_1=0$. As $f$ is surjective on generic stalks and equivariant for $I_0$, the representation $F_{\mathcal K}(0)$ is a quotient of $(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})(0)$, hence tame. By Step~2 it is therefore unipotent, with $r(n-1)$ blocks of size $2$ and $\kappa_1$ blocks of size $1$. So it has dimension $2r(n-1)+\kappa_1=r(n)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:binomial}. Thus $F_{\mathcal K}$ and $\mathcal W_n|_U$ both have rank $r(n)$, and $f$, a surjection of lisse sheaves of the same rank, is an isomorphism. Hence $\mathcal N|_U=(\ker f)[1]=0$, so $\mathcal N$ is supported on the finite set $C_c\smallsetminus U$, that is, punctual. As $\mathcal N$ is a subobject of $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}[1]$, it vanishes by (P3). Therefore $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}[1]\to\mathcal K$ is an isomorphism, which is (i). Statements (ii) and (iii) now follow from Step 2. Moreover, by \eqref{eq:GOS}, $\operatorname{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})=\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_m,\mathcal K)-\operatorname{Swan}_0(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})=2^{n-1}$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:euler-H}
One has $\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_m\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mathcal H_n|_{C_c})=-2^{n-1}$, and the Swan conductors at $\infty$ of $\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}$ and of $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}$ are both equal to $2^{n-1}$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal N_c$ be the sheaf of Lemma~\ref{lem:conv-model} on $X_c=\mathbb{G}_{m,t}\times\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}$, so that $\mathcal N_c(t,h_1)=\mathrm{Kl}(h_1t)\otimes\mathcal M_c(t)$. Compactly supported Euler characteristics are compatible with $R(-)_!$, by the Leray spectral sequence. By Lemma~\ref{lem:conv-model}, $R\operatorname{pr}_{h_1!}\mathcal N_c\cong\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}[-1]$, so $\chi_c(X_c\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mathcal N_c)=-\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_m\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mathcal H_n|_{C_c})$. On the other hand, the automorphism $(t,h_1)\mapsto(t,h_1t)$ of $X_c$ commutes with $\operatorname{pr}_t$ and carries $\mathcal N_c$ to $\mathcal M_c\boxtimes\mathrm{Kl}$. By the K\"unneth formula, $R\operatorname{pr}_{t!}\mathcal N_c\cong\mathcal M_c\otimes R\Gamma_c(\mathbb{G}_m\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mathrm{Kl})$, and $R\Gamma_c(\mathbb{G}_m\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mathrm{Kl})$ is a line placed in degree $1$, by (K1)--(K3) and~\eqref{eq:GOS}. Hence $\chi_c(X_c\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mathcal N_c)=-\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_m\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mathcal M_c)$. The sheaf $\mathcal M_c$ is tame at $0$, and all its $2^{n-1}$ breaks at $\infty$ equal $1$, as shown in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:local-data}(ii), so $\chi_c(\mathbb{G}_m\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mathcal M_c)=-2^{n-1}$ by~\eqref{eq:GOS}. This proves the first assertion. By~\eqref{eq:GOS} and Proposition~\ref{prop:tame}, $\operatorname{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal H_n|_{C_c})=2^{n-1}$. Finally, $\mathcal H_n|_{C_c}$ is a successive extension of $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}$, of the constant sheaf $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$ and of the sheaves $\operatorname{gr}^{\mathrm W}_{2k}\mathcal G_n|_{C_c}$, which are geometrically constant by Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse}(vi). Swan conductors are additive in exact sequences, and they vanish on geometrically constant sheaves; so $\operatorname{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})=2^{n-1}$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:R-global}
There is a lisse sheaf $F$ on $U_v=\mathbb{G}_{m,v}\smallsetminus\{s\}$ with $\mathcal R|_{U_v}\cong F[-(n-2)]$, and $F$ extends to a lisse sheaf on $\mathbb P^1_v\smallsetminus\{0,s\}$. In particular the inertia group at $v=\infty$ acts trivially on the generic stalk of $F$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
For $v\in U_v$ put $a(v)=\frac{\lambda v}{\lambda v+1}\,c\in\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}$; this is defined because $v\ne0$ and $\lambda v+1\ne0$. For $u'\in\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}$, the conditions $u'\in U$ and $b(u')=v$ mean $\sum_{i\ge2}c_iu_i=-(\lambda+v^{-1})$, and this equation is equivalent to $\langle a(v),u'\rangle=-\lambda$. Hence $b^{-1}(U_v)$ is the inverse image under $a$ of the universal family $\mathcal Y_{n-1}=\{(h',u'):\langle h',u'\rangle=-\lambda\}$ over $\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}$ of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:tame}, with the same phase $f'$. In the coordinate $w=v^{-1}$ we have $a=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+w}\,c$, which extends to $w=0$, that is, to $v=\infty$, with value $c$. Suppose $n\ge3$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:integrate-t} and Theorem~\ref{thm:lisse}(iii) for $n-1$ variables, the direct image of $\mathcal{L}_\psi(f')$ along $\mathcal Y_{n-1}\to\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}$ is $\mathcal G_{n-1}(1)[-(n-2)]$, and proper base change gives the assertions with $F=a^*\mathcal G_{n-1}(1)$. If $n=2$, the fibre of $b$ over $v\in U_v$ is the point $u_2=-(\lambda+v^{-1})/c_2$, and $F=\mathcal{L}_\psi(-c_2v/(\lambda v+1))$, which is lisse on $\mathbb P^1_v\smallsetminus\{s\}$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:slopes-infinity}
Every break of $(\mathcal G_n|_{C_c})(\infty)$ is at most $1$. If $M$ is the part of $(\mathcal G_n|_{C_c})(\infty)$ of break $1$, then all breaks of $\mathcal{L}_\psi(h_1/\lambda)(\infty)\otimes M$ are $<1$. The same holds for every subquotient of $\mathcal G_n|_{C_c}$, in particular for $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Let $\mathfrak C$ be the class of continuous representations $Q$ of the inertia group at $\infty$ such that all breaks of $Q$ are $\le1$ and all breaks of $\mathcal{L}_\psi(h_1/\lambda)(\infty)\otimes Q^{(1)}$ are $<1$, where $Q^{(1)}$ is the part of $Q$ of break $1$. The break decomposition is functorial and exact \cite[1.1]{Katz-Gauss}, so $\mathfrak C$ is stable under subquotients and extensions. It contains every representation all of whose breaks are $<1$, and every representation $\mathcal{L}_\psi(sh_1)(\infty)\otimes Y$ with all breaks of $Y$ less than $1$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:breaks}(ii); recall $s=-1/\lambda$.

Let $j_U\colon\mathbb A^1_v\smallsetminus\{0,s\}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1_v$ be the inclusion, let $F$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:R-global}, and put $K_1=j_{U!}F[1]$. The complex $j_{v!}\mathcal R$ vanishes at $v=0$ and agrees with $F[-(n-2)]$ on $U_v$. So excision for the point $s$ gives a distinguished triangle
\[
K_1[-(n-1)]\longrightarrow j_{v!}\mathcal R\longrightarrow i_{s*}\mathcal R_s\longrightarrow,
\]
where $\mathcal R_s$ is the stalk of $\mathcal R$ at $s$, a complex of finite-dimensional vector spaces. By proper base change, $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(i_{s*}\mathcal R_s)\cong\mathcal R_s\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(sh_1)[1]$, whose cohomology sheaves are of the form $\mathcal{L}_\psi(sh_1)\otimes(\text{constant})$. By~\eqref{eq:stationary}, applied with $\Sigma=\{0,s\}$ and $F_\Sigma=F$, the representation $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K_1)(\infty)$ lies in $\mathfrak C$: the summand for $x=0$ has all breaks $<1$, the summand for $x=s$ is of the form $\mathcal{L}_\psi(sh_1)(\infty)\otimes Y$ with all breaks of $Y$ less than $1$, and the last summand vanishes, because $F(\infty)$ is trivial by Lemma~\ref{lem:R-global}. Here $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K_1)(\infty)$ denotes the representation on the generic stalk of the lisse sheaf $\mathcal H^{-1}(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K_1))$ near $\infty$; the sheaf $\mathcal H^0(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K_1))$ is punctual, since $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K_1)$ is perverse \cite[(1.3.2.3)]{Laumon}.

Apply $\operatorname{FT}_\psi$ to the triangle. By~\eqref{eq:FT-model}, $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(j_{v!}\mathcal R)$ is, on $\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}$, the lisse sheaf $\mathcal G_n|_{C_c}(1)$ placed in degree $n-2$. On a punctured neighbourhood of $\infty$ all cohomology sheaves involved are lisse, $\mathcal H^{n-2}\big(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K_1)[-(n-1)]\big)=\mathcal H^{-1}(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K_1))$, and $\mathcal H^{n-1}\big(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K_1)[-(n-1)]\big)=\mathcal H^0(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K_1))$ vanishes there. So the long exact sequence of cohomology sheaves exhibits $(\mathcal G_n|_{C_c})(\infty)$ as an extension of a submodule of $\mathcal H^{n-2}\big(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(i_{s*}\mathcal R_s)\big)(\infty)$ by a quotient of $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K_1)(\infty)$. Tate twists do not change the action of inertia. Since $\mathfrak C$ is stable under subquotients and extensions, $(\mathcal G_n|_{C_c})(\infty)$ and all its subquotients lie in $\mathfrak C$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:infinity}
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})(\infty)=T\oplus M$, where $T$ is the tame part, unipotent of dimension $r(n)-2^{n-1}$ with $\kappa_j$ Jordan blocks of size $j-2$ for each $j\ge3$, and $M$ has dimension $2^{n-1}$ and is isoclinic of break $1$. Moreover $M\cong\mathcal{L}_\psi(-h_1/\lambda)(\infty)\otimes X$, where all breaks of $X$ are $<1$.
\item The sheaf $\det(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}h_1)$ on $C_c$ is geometrically constant.
\end{enumerate}
In particular Theorem~\ref{thmC}(ii) and~(iii) hold.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
(i) By Theorem~\ref{thm:boundary}(iii), the tame part $T$ is unipotent with $\kappa_j$ blocks of size $j-2$ for $j\ge3$. Since $\sum_jj\kappa_j=2^{n-1}$ and $\sum_j\kappa_j=\binom{n-1}{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}$,
\[
\dim T=\sum_{j\ge3}(j-2)\kappa_j=2^{n-1}-2\binom{n-1}{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}+\kappa_1=r(n)-2^{n-1},
\]
the last equality by Lemma~\ref{lem:binomial}. So the wild part of $(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})(\infty)$ has dimension $2^{n-1}$, and its breaks are positive and add up to $\operatorname{Swan}_\infty(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})=2^{n-1}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:boundary}(iii)). By Proposition~\ref{prop:slopes-infinity} they are at most $1$, so they all equal $1$. Thus the wild part is the part $M$ of break $1$, and $X=\mathcal{L}_\psi(h_1/\lambda)(\infty)\otimes M$ has all breaks $<1$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:slopes-infinity}.

(ii) Put $\mathcal D=\det(\mathcal W_n|_{C_c})\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}h_1)$, a lisse sheaf of rank one on $C_c\cong\mathbb{G}_m$, and work over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$. At $h_1=0$ the local monodromy of $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}$ is unipotent (Theorem~\ref{thm:boundary}(ii)), so its determinant is trivial on $I_0$; as $\mathcal{L}_\psi(2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}h_1)$ is lisse at $0$, the sheaf $\mathcal D$ extends to a lisse sheaf $\bar{\mathcal D}$ on $\mathbb A^1$. At $\infty$, by (i),
\[
\mathcal D(\infty)\cong\det T\otimes\det\big(\mathcal{L}_\psi(-h_1/\lambda)(\infty)\otimes X\big)\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}h_1)(\infty)=\det T\otimes\det X.
\]
The character $\det T$ is tame, and $\det X$, a direct summand of $X^{\otimes2^{n-1}}$, has break $<1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:breaks}(i). So $\operatorname{Swan}_\infty(\bar{\mathcal D})<1$, and the Grothendieck--Ogg--Shafarevich formula on $\mathbb A^1$ \cite[Exp.~X]{SGA5} gives $\chi_c(\mathbb A^1\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\bar{\mathcal D})=1-\operatorname{Swan}_\infty(\bar{\mathcal D})>0$. Since $H^0_c$ vanishes, $H^2_c(\mathbb A^1\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\bar{\mathcal D})\ne0$; that is, the rank-one sheaf $\bar{\mathcal D}$ has nonzero geometric coinvariants, and it is geometrically constant.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:V2}
Let $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_q$. Then $\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_q}K(ax)$ equals $-q$ if $a=0$ and $0$ otherwise. Moreover
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_q}K(ax)K(bx)=\begin{cases}q^2-q,&a=b\ne0,\\-q,&a\ne b,\ ab\ne0,\\0,&\text{exactly one of $a,b$ is }0,\\q,&a=b=0.\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
We have $\sum_{y\in\mathbb{F}_q}K(y)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times}\psi_q(x^{-1})\sum_{y\in\mathbb{F}_q}\psi_q(xy)=0$, which gives the first assertion, as $K(0)=-1$. If $a,b\ne0$, expanding and summing over $x$ first gives
\[
\sum_xK(ax)K(bx)=q\sum_{\substack{u,v\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times\\au+bv=0}}\psi_q(u^{-1}+v^{-1})=q\sum_{u\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times}\psi_q\big((1-b/a)u^{-1}\big),
\]
which is $q(q-1)$ if $a=b$ and $-q$ otherwise. If $a=0\ne b$, the sum is $-\sum_xK(bx)=0$, and if $a=b=0$ it is $q$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:low-moments}
For every $n\ge2$,
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}\Sigma_n(h)=(-1)^nq^{n-1}$;
\item $\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}|\Sigma_n(h)|^2=q^{n-2}\big((q-1)^{n+1}+1-(-1)^n(q-2)\big)$;
\item $\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}\Sigma_n(h)^2=q^{n-2}\big(1-(q-1)^n+2(-1)^n\big)$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular Theorem~\ref{thmD}(i) holds.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Expand each factor $\Sigma_n(h)$ by~\eqref{eq:intro-factor} and sum over $h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n$; the sum over $h$ factors over the coordinates. For (i), this gives $q\sum_h\Sigma_n(h)=\sum_t\psi_q(\lambda t)\big(\sum_xK(tx)\big)^n=(-q)^n$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:V2}. For (ii) and (iii), put $V_2(t_1,t_2)=\sum_xK(t_1x)K(t_2x)$. Since $K$ is real,
\[
\begin{aligned}
q^2\sum_h|\Sigma_n(h)|^2&=\sum_{t_1,t_2}\psi_q\big(\lambda(t_1-t_2)\big)V_2(t_1,t_2)^n,\\
q^2\sum_h\Sigma_n(h)^2&=\sum_{t_1,t_2}\psi_q\big(\lambda(t_1+t_2)\big)V_2(t_1,t_2)^n.
\end{aligned}
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:V2}, the pair $t_1=t_2=0$ contributes $q^n$, pairs with exactly one zero coordinate contribute $0$, pairs with $t_1=t_2\ne0$ contribute $(q^2-q)^n$ times $\psi_q(0)=1$, respectively times $\psi_q(2\lambda t_1)$, and pairs with $t_1\ne t_2$ and $t_1t_2\ne0$ contribute $(-q)^n$ times the additive character. Since $\sum_{t\ne0}\psi_q(c\,t)=-1$ for $c\ne0$, and $2\lambda\ne0$,
\[
\sum_{\substack{t_1\ne t_2\\t_1t_2\ne0}}\psi_q\big(\lambda(t_1-t_2)\big)=1-(q-1)=2-q,\qquad\sum_{\substack{t_1\ne t_2\\t_1t_2\ne0}}\psi_q\big(\lambda(t_1+t_2)\big)=1-(-1)=2.
\]
Hence $q^2\sum_h|\Sigma_n(h)|^2=q^n+(q-1)(q^2-q)^n+(2-q)(-q)^n$ and $q^2\sum_h\Sigma_n(h)^2=q^n-(q^2-q)^n+2(-q)^n$, which are (ii) and (iii).
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:master}
For every $n\ge2$,
\[
q^4\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}|\Sigma_n(h)|^4=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{F}_q^4}\psi_q(\Lambda(t))\,V(t)^n.
\]
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Write $|\Sigma_n(h)|^4=\Sigma_n(h)\overline{\Sigma_n(h)}\Sigma_n(h)\overline{\Sigma_n(h)}$ and expand each factor by \eqref{eq:intro-factor}, with summation variables $t_1,\dots,t_4$. Since $K$ is real, conjugation only replaces $\psi_q(\lambda t_j)$ by $\psi_q(-\lambda t_j)$, so the additive phases combine to $\Lambda(t)$. The remaining product $\prod_{i,j}K(t_jh_i)$ factors over $i$, and summing over $h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n$ gives $V(t)^n$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:diag}
Let $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times$, $\rho=a/b$, and let $\chi_2$ be the quadratic character of $\mathbb{F}_q^\times$, extended by $\chi_2(0)=0$. Then
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_q}K(ax)^2K(bx)^2=\begin{cases}2q^3-3q^2-3q,&\rho=1,\\ q^3-(2+\chi_2(\rho))q^2-3q,&\rho\ne1.\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
For $s\in\mathbb{F}_q$ let $\tau(s)$ be the sum of $\psi_q(x_1^{-1}+x_2^{-1})$ over $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ with $x_1+x_2=s$. Expanding the squares gives $K(y)^2=\sum_s\tau(s)\psi_q(ys)$, and orthogonality in $x$ yields
\[
\sum_xK(ax)^2K(bx)^2=q\sum_{s\in\mathbb{F}_q}\tau(s)\tau(-\rho s).
\]
Clearly $\tau(0)=q-1$. For $s\ne0$ write $x_1=sy$ and $x_2=s(1-y)$ with $y\notin\{0,1\}$; then $x_1^{-1}+x_2^{-1}=\big(sy(1-y)\big)^{-1}$. For $m\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ the equation $y(1-y)=m$ has $1+\chi_2(1-4m)$ solutions. Hence, writing $\mu=m^{-1}$ and noting $\chi_2(1-4m)=\chi_2(\mu(\mu-4))$,
\[
\tau(s)=\sum_{m\ne0}\big(1+\chi_2(1-4m)\big)\psi_q\Big(\frac1{sm}\Big)=-1+R(s),\qquad R(s)=\sum_{\mu\ne0}\chi_2\big(\mu(\mu-4)\big)\psi_q(\mu/s).
\]
We use Jacobsthal's evaluation: $\sum_{\mu\in\mathbb{F}_q}\chi_2\big((\mu-\alpha)(\mu-\beta)\big)=-1$ for distinct $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}_q$. Indeed, for $\mu\ne\beta$ the summand is $\chi_2(z)$ with $z=(\mu-\alpha)/(\mu-\beta)$, which runs over $\mathbb{F}_q\smallsetminus\{1\}$. Since $p$ is odd, $0\ne4$, so $\sum_{\mu\ne0}\chi_2(\mu(\mu-4))=-1$, and therefore $\sum_{s\ne0}R(s)=\sum_{s\ne0}R(-\rho s)=1$. Moreover
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{s\ne0}R(s)R(-\rho s)&=\sum_{\mu,\mu'\ne0}\chi_2\big(\mu(\mu-4)\big)\chi_2\big(\mu'(\mu'-4)\big)\big(q\,\mathbf 1_{\mu'=\rho\mu}-1\big)\\
&=q\,\chi_2(\rho)\sum_{\mu\ne0}\chi_2\big((\mu-4)(\rho\mu-4)\big)-1.
\end{aligned}
\]
If $\rho\ne1$, Jacobsthal's evaluation with the roots $4$ and $4/\rho$ gives $\sum_{\mu\ne0}\chi_2\big((\mu-4)(\rho\mu-4)\big)=-\chi_2(\rho)-1$, so the last expression equals $-q-q\chi_2(\rho)-1$. If $\rho=1$ the sum is $q-2$, and the expression equals $q^2-2q-1$. Finally
\[
\sum_s\tau(s)\tau(-\rho s)=(q-1)^2+(q-1)-2+\sum_{s\ne0}R(s)R(-\rho s),
\]
which is $q^2-2q-3-q\chi_2(\rho)$ if $\rho\ne1$ and $2q^2-3q-3$ if $\rho=1$. Multiplying by $q$ gives the lemma.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:diag-main}
For $n\ge2$, $\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_D}\psi_q(\Lambda(t))V(t)^n=2q^{3n+2}+O(q^{3n+1})$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
On $\mathcal T_D$ we have $\Lambda=0$ and $V(a,a,b,b)=V(a,b,b,a)=\sum_xK(ax)^2K(bx)^2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:diag} this is $q^3+O(q^2)$ for the $(q-1)(q-2)$ pairs with $a\ne b$, and $2q^3+O(q^2)$ for the $q-1$ pairs with $a=b$. Hence each of $\mathcal D_1$ and $\mathcal D_2$ contributes $q^{3n+2}+O(q^{3n+1})$, while their intersection, the diagonal, contributes $O(q^{3n+1})$. Inclusion--exclusion gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:pair}
For $n\ge2$, $\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_P}\psi_q(\Lambda(t))V(t)^n=O(q^{3n+1})$.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
For $t=(a,b,a,b)$ with $a\ne b$, Lemma~\ref{lem:diag} gives $V(t)=q^3+O(q^2)$, hence $V(t)^n=q^{3n}+O(q^{3n-1})$, while $\Lambda(t)=2\lambda(a-b)$. Since $2\lambda\ne0$,
\[
\sum_{\substack{a,b\ne0\\a\ne b}}\psi_q\big(2\lambda(a-b)\big)=\Big|\sum_{a\ne0}\psi_q(2\lambda a)\Big|^2-(q-1)=2-q.
\]
So the main term contributes $O(q^{3n+1})$. The error term, summed trivially over $O(q^2)$ points, contributes $O(q^{3n+1})$ as well.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:zero}
For $n\ge2$, $\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_0}\psi_q(\Lambda(t))V(t)^n=O\big(q^{(5n+6)/2}\big)$.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Suppose exactly $a\le3$ coordinates of $t$ are nonzero. The term $x=0$ of $V(t)$ has absolute value $1$, and Weil's bound gives $|V(t)|\le1+(q-1)2^aq^{a/2}\le2^{a+1}q^{1+a/2}$. There are at most $\binom4aq^a$ such $t$. The resulting bound $O\big(q^{a+n(1+a/2)}\big)$ is largest for $a=3$, where it equals $O\big(q^{(5n+6)/2}\big)$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:plane}
If all $t_i\ne0$, then $V(t)=-q^2\big(a_t+2+3q^{-1}\big)$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Orthogonality in $x$ gives $V(t)=q\,\Sigma_0(t)$, where $\Sigma_0(t)$ is the sum of $\psi_q(u_1^{-1}+\cdots+u_4^{-1})$ over the $u\in(\mathbb{F}_q^\times)^4$ with $\sum_it_iu_i=0$. This set is stable under scalar multiplication, and summing $\psi_q(\nu^{-1}f(u))$ over $\nu\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ gives $q-1$ if $f(u)=0$ and $-1$ otherwise. Hence $\Sigma_0(t)=qN_0-N$, where $N$ is the number of points of $H_t(\mathbb{F}_q)$ with no zero coordinate and $N_0$ is the number of those with $f(u)=0$. The four lines $H_t\cap\{u_i=0\}$ are distinct. They meet pairwise in the six points of $H_t$ with exactly two zero coordinates, and no three of them are concurrent, since $H_t$ contains no coordinate point. Inclusion--exclusion gives $N=(q^2+q+1)-4(q+1)+6=q^2-3q+3$. For $u$ with no zero coordinate, $f(u)=0$ if and only if $e_3(u)=0$. The restriction of $e_3$ to $\{u_i=0\}$ is the product of the other three coordinates. So a point of $\Gamma_t$ with a zero coordinate has exactly two zero coordinates, and each of the six such points of $H_t$ lies on $\mathcal Q$. Hence $N_0=\#\Gamma_t(\mathbb{F}_q)-6=q-5-a_t$, so $\Sigma_0(t)=-qa_t-2q-3$, and the formula follows.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:lines}
The lines of $\mathbb P^3$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q$ contained in $\mathcal Q$ are exactly the six coordinate edges $\{u_i=u_j=0\}$ and the three lines $\{u_i+u_j=u_k+u_l=0\}$, $\{i,j\}\sqcup\{k,l\}=\{1,2,3,4\}$. For $t\in\mathcal T_G$ the curve $\Gamma_t$ is a geometrically irreducible and reduced plane cubic.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Throughout the proof, points and lines are taken over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q$. The nine lines lie on $\mathcal Q$. Every monomial of $e_3$ involves $u_i$ or $u_j$, so $e_3$ vanishes on $\{u_i=u_j=0\}$. For a partition $\{i,j\}\sqcup\{k,l\}$ one has $e_3=u_iu_j(u_k+u_l)+u_ku_l(u_i+u_j)$, which vanishes on $\{u_i+u_j=u_k+u_l=0\}$. Conversely, a line through the point $(1:0:0:0)$ consists of the points $(1:sa:sb:sc)$ together with $(0:a:b:c)$. It lies on $\mathcal Q$ if and only if $s^2(ab+ac+bc)+s^3abc$ vanishes identically, that is, if and only if two of $a,b,c$ vanish. By symmetry, the lines on $\mathcal Q$ through a coordinate point are the coordinate edges. A line contained in a coordinate plane $u_i=0$ lies on $\mathcal Q$ only if the product of the other three coordinates vanishes on it, so it is again a coordinate edge.

Let $\Pi\subset\mathcal Q$ be a line through no coordinate point and not contained in a coordinate plane. Each $u_i$ restricts to a nonzero linear form $\theta_i$ on $\Pi\cong\mathbb P^1$, with a single zero $z_i$. Choose an affine coordinate $z$ on $\Pi$ for which no $z_i$ lies at infinity, and write $\theta_i=\alpha_i(z-z_i)$ with $\alpha_i\ne0$. Since $e_3=\theta_1\theta_2\theta_3\theta_4\sum_i\theta_i^{-1}$ on $\Pi$, the rational function $\sum_i\alpha_i^{-1}(z-z_i)^{-1}$ vanishes identically. A zero $z_i$ distinct from all the others would be a simple pole with residue $\alpha_i^{-1}\ne0$, so the zeros coincide at least in pairs. Three of them cannot coincide, for $\Pi$ would then pass through a coordinate point. Thus, after renumbering, $z_1=z_2\ne z_3=z_4$, and $\theta_2=\gamma\theta_1$, $\theta_4=\gamma'\theta_3$ with $\gamma,\gamma'\ne0$. Then
\[
e_3|_\Pi=\theta_1\theta_3\big(\gamma(1+\gamma')\theta_1+\gamma'(1+\gamma)\theta_3\big),
\]
and since $\theta_1,\theta_3$ are linearly independent, $\gamma=\gamma'=-1$. So $\Pi$ is the line $u_1+u_2=u_3+u_4=0$.

Now let $t\in\mathcal T_G$. The plane $H_t$ contains no coordinate edge, since $\{u_i=u_j=0\}\subset H_t$ would force $t_k=t_l=0$. It contains the line $u_i+u_j=u_k+u_l=0$, which is spanned by $e_i-e_j$ and $e_k-e_l$, if and only if $t_i=t_j$ and $t_k=t_l$. For the three partitions these conditions describe exactly $\mathcal D_1$, $\mathcal D_2$ and $\mathcal T_P\cup(\mathcal D_1\cap\mathcal D_2)$. Hence $H_t$ contains no line of $\mathcal Q$. In particular $H_t\not\subset\mathcal Q$, so $\Gamma_t$ is a plane cubic curve. A plane cubic that is reducible or non-reduced over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q$ contains a line, which would be a line of $\mathcal Q$ lying in $H_t$. Hence $\Gamma_t$ is geometrically irreducible and reduced.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:hasse}
For $t\in\mathcal T_G$, $|a_t|\le2q^{1/2}$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
The six points of $H_t$ with exactly two zero coordinates are $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational points of $\Gamma_t$, and they are smooth points of $\Gamma_t$. For instance, at $(t_2:-t_1:0:0)$ the gradient of $e_3$ is $(0,0,u_1u_2,u_1u_2)$ with $u_1u_2\ne0$, and it is not proportional to the gradient $(t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4)$ of the equation of $H_t$, because $t_1\ne0$. If $\Gamma_t$ is smooth, it is therefore an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{F}_q$, and Hasse's theorem \cite[Ch.~V, Th.~1.1]{Silverman} gives $|a_t|\le2q^{1/2}$. Otherwise $\Gamma_t$ is, by Proposition~\ref{prop:lines}, a geometrically irreducible singular plane cubic. A line through two singular points, or through a point of multiplicity $3$ and a further point of $\Gamma_t$, would meet $\Gamma_t$ with total multiplicity at least $4$. By B\'ezout's theorem it would then be a component of $\Gamma_t$, which is impossible. Hence $\Gamma_t$ has a unique singular point $P_0$, and it is a double point. Being unique, $P_0$ is fixed by $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q/\mathbb{F}_q)$ and is $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational. Let $\nu\colon\tilde\Gamma\to\Gamma_t$ be the normalization. The arithmetic genus of a plane cubic is $1$, and the double point lowers it by at least $1$, so $\tilde\Gamma$ is a smooth projective curve of genus $0$. It has an $\mathbb{F}_q$-point, lying above a smooth rational point of $\Gamma_t$, so it is isomorphic to $\mathbb P^1$. The map $\nu$ is an isomorphism away from $P_0$, and $\nu^{-1}(P_0)$ consists of one or two geometric points, one for each branch of $\Gamma_t$ at $P_0$. Hence $\nu^{-1}(P_0)$ has $0$, $1$ or $2$ rational points. Therefore $\#\Gamma_t(\mathbb{F}_q)=(q+1-\#\nu^{-1}(P_0)(\mathbb{F}_q))+1$, and $a_t=\#\nu^{-1}(P_0)(\mathbb{F}_q)-1$ satisfies $|a_t|\le1$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:ray}
For every integer $k\ge0$,
\[
\Big|\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_G}\psi_q(\Lambda(t))\,a_t^k\Big|\le7\cdot2^kq^{3+k/2}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Let $\nu\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times$. The sets $\mathcal T_0$, $\mathcal D_1$, $\mathcal D_2$ and $\mathcal T_P$ are defined by conditions invariant under $t\mapsto\nu t$: the vanishing of a coordinate, and the patterns $(a,a,b,b)$, $(a,b,b,a)$ and $(a,b,a,b)$ with $a\ne b$. Hence $\mathcal T_G$ is stable under $t\mapsto\nu t$. Moreover $H_{\nu t}=H_t$, so $\Gamma_{\nu t}=\Gamma_t$ and $a_{\nu t}=a_t$; and $\Lambda(\nu t)=\nu\Lambda(t)$, as $\Lambda$ is linear. All coordinates of a point $t\in\mathcal T_G$ are nonzero, so $\nu t=t$ forces $\nu=1$. Thus $\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ acts freely on $\mathcal T_G$, and $\mathcal T_G$ is the disjoint union of the orbits $\{\nu t:\nu\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times\}$, each with $q-1$ elements. Let $\overline{\mathcal T}_G\subset\mathbb P^3(\mathbb{F}_q)$ be the set of orbits, that is, the image of $\mathcal T_G$. The condition $\Lambda(t)=0$ depends only on the orbit $[t]$, and
\[
\sum_{\nu\in\mathbb{F}_q^\times}\psi_q(\nu\Lambda(t))=\begin{cases}q-1,&\Lambda(t)=0,\\-1,&\Lambda(t)\ne0.\end{cases}
\]
Summing first over each orbit, we obtain
\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_G}\psi_q(\Lambda(t))\,a_t^k=(q-1)\sum_{\substack{[t]\in\overline{\mathcal T}_G\\ \Lambda(t)=0}}a_t^k-\sum_{\substack{[t]\in\overline{\mathcal T}_G\\ \Lambda(t)\ne0}}a_t^k=q\sum_{\substack{[t]\in\overline{\mathcal T}_G\\ \Lambda(t)=0}}a_t^k-\sum_{[t]\in\overline{\mathcal T}_G}a_t^k.
\]
The orbits with $\Lambda(t)=0$ lie on the plane $\Lambda=0$ of $\mathbb P^3$, which has $q^2+q+1\le3q^2$ rational points, and $\#\overline{\mathcal T}_G\le\#\mathbb P^3(\mathbb{F}_q)=q^3+q^2+q+1\le4q^3$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:hasse}, $|a_t|^k\le(2q^{1/2})^k$ for every $[t]\in\overline{\mathcal T}_G$. So the right-hand side is at most $(q\cdot3q^2+4q^3)(2q^{1/2})^k=7\cdot2^kq^{3+k/2}$ in absolute value.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:generic}
For $n\ge2$, $\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_G}\psi_q(\Lambda(t))V(t)^n=O\big(q^{(5n+6)/2}\big)$.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:plane}, $V(t)^n=(-1)^nq^{2n}\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk(2+3q^{-1})^{n-k}a_t^k$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:ray} to each term; the largest contribution, $O(q^{2n+3+n/2})$, comes from $k=n$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:fourth}
For every $n\ge3$,
\[
\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}|\Sigma_n(h)|^4=2q^{3n-2}+O\big(q^{3n-2-\delta(n)}\big).
\]
In particular Theorem~\ref{thmD}(ii) holds.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
The four strata partition $\mathbb{F}_q^4$, and Table~\ref{tab:strata} collects their contributions to the right-hand side of Proposition~\ref{prop:master}. Adding them, the left-hand side multiplied by $q^4$ equals $2q^{3n+2}+O(q^{3n+1})+O\big(q^{(5n+6)/2}\big)$. After division by $q^4$ the main term is $2q^{3n-2}$, and the two error terms are $O(q^{A_1})$ and $O(q^{A_2})$ with
\[
A_1=3n-3=(3n-2)-1,\qquad A_2=\frac{5n-2}2=(3n-2)-\frac{n-2}2.
\]
So the total error is $O(q^{3n-2-\delta(n)})$ with $\delta(n)=\min\big(1,\frac{n-2}2\big)$. For $n=3$ one has $A_1=6$ and $A_2=\frac{13}2$, so $\delta(3)=\frac12$; for $n\ge4$, $A_2\le A_1$ and $\delta(n)=1$.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:lower}
Let $n\ge3$. As $q\to\infty$ through powers of $p$,
\[
q^{-n}\sum_{h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)}|A^0_q(h)|^4=2+O\big(q^{-1/2}\big).
\]
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
By~\eqref{eq:normalized}, $\big||\Sigma_n(h)|^4-q^{2n-2}|A^0_q(h)|^4\big|\ll q^{3(n-1)/2}q^{(n-2)/2}=q^{2n-5/2}$, and summing over the at most $q^n$ points of $S(\mathbb{F}_q)$,
\[
\sum_{h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)}|\Sigma_n(h)|^4=q^{2n-2}\sum_{h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)}|A^0_q(h)|^4+O(q^{3n-5/2}).
\]
The points of $\mathbb{F}_q^n\smallsetminus S(\mathbb{F}_q)$ contribute $O(q^{3n-5})$ to the fourth moment. Since $\delta(n)\ge\frac12$ for $n\ge3$, Theorem~\ref{thm:fourth} yields $q^{2n-2}\sum_{h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)}|A^0_q(h)|^4=2q^{3n-2}+O(q^{3n-5/2})$.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{prop:moment}
Let $T$ be a smooth geometrically connected variety of dimension $d$ over a finite field $\mathbb F_{q_0}$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a lisse sheaf on $T$, pure of weight $w$, with geometric generic stalk $V_{\mathcal F}$ and geometric monodromy group $G_{\mathcal F}$. Put $M=M_4(G_{\mathcal F},V_{\mathcal F})$. Then there are complex numbers $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_M$ of absolute value $1$ such that, for $q=q_0^k$,
\[
q^{-d}\sum_{x\in T(\mathbb{F}_q)}\big|q^{-w/2}\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_x\mid\mathcal F)\big|^4=\sum_{m=1}^M\beta_m^k+O\big(q^{-1/2}\big).
\]
Consequently, if the left-hand side tends to a limit $L$ as $k\to\infty$, then $L=M$.
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Put $\mathcal E=\mathcal F^{\otimes2}\otimes(\mathcal F^\vee)^{\otimes2}$, a lisse sheaf pure of weight $0$. At $x\in T(\mathbb{F}_q)$ the eigenvalues of $\operatorname{Frob}_x$ on $\mathcal F^\vee$ are the inverses $\alpha^{-1}=q^{-w}\bar\alpha$ of the eigenvalues $\alpha$ on $\mathcal F$, so $\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_x\mid\mathcal E)=\big|q^{-w/2}\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Frob}_x\mid\mathcal F)\big|^4$. The invariants of $\pi_1(T\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q)$ on $V_{\mathcal F}^{\otimes2}\otimes(V_{\mathcal F}^\vee)^{\otimes2}$ are those of its Zariski closure $G_{\mathcal F}$, and they have dimension $M$. Lemma~\ref{lem:averages} gives the assertions.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:M4}
For $n\ge3$ one has $M_4(G,V)=2$. Consequently $V$ is an irreducible representation of $G$, and it is not self-dual.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:lower} and Proposition~\ref{prop:moment}, applied to $\mathcal W_n$ on $T=S$ with $d=n$ and $w=n+1$, give $M_4(G,V)=2$. Since $V$ is semisimple, if it were reducible we could write $V=V_1\oplus V_2$ with $V_1,V_2\ne0$ stable under $G$; then $\dim\operatorname{End}_G(V)\ge2$, and the injection $\operatorname{End}_G(V)\otimes\operatorname{End}_G(V)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{End}_G(V\otimes V)$ gives $M_4\ge4$. Suppose $V\cong V^\vee$. Since $V$ is irreducible, $(V\otimes V)^G\cong\operatorname{Hom}_G(V^\vee,V)$ is one-dimensional by Schur's lemma. Write $V\otimes V=\operatorname{Sym}^2V\oplus\bigwedge^2V$; both summands are $G$-stable. The two components of an invariant vector are invariant, so the invariant line lies in $\operatorname{Sym}^2V$ or in $\bigwedge^2V$, say in $X$, and let $Y$ be the other summand. Put $N=\dim V=r(n)\ge5$. Then $\dim\operatorname{Sym}^2V=N(N+1)/2$ and $\dim\bigwedge^2V=N(N-1)/2$ both exceed $1$. Hence $X=\mathbf 1\oplus X'$ with $X'\ne0$, and $Y\ne0$. So $V\otimes V=\mathbf 1\oplus X'\oplus Y$ with three nonzero $G$-stable summands. The three projections are linearly independent elements of $\operatorname{End}_G(V\otimes V)$, so $M_4\ge3$.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:M2}
Let $n\ge2$. As $q\to\infty$ through powers of $p$,
\[
q^{-n}\sum_{h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)}|A^0_q(h)|^2=1+O\big(q^{-1/2}\big),\qquad q^{-n}\sum_{h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)}A^0_q(h)^2=O\big(q^{-1/2}\big).
\]
Consequently $\dim\operatorname{End}_G(V)=1$ and $(V\otimes V)^G=0$: the representation $V$ of $G$ is irreducible and not self-dual.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
By~\eqref{eq:normalized}, for $h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)$,
\[
|\Sigma_n(h)|^2=q^{n-1}|A^0_q(h)|^2+2c_n(q)q^{(n-1)/2}\operatorname{Re}A^0_q(h)+c_n(q)^2,
\]
and similarly $\Sigma_n(h)^2=q^{n-1}A^0_q(h)^2+2c_n(q)q^{(n-1)/2}A^0_q(h)+c_n(q)^2$. Summed over the at most $q^n$ points of $S(\mathbb{F}_q)$, the last two terms contribute $O(q^{(n-2)/2+(n-1)/2+n})=O(q^{2n-3/2})$. The points outside $S(\mathbb{F}_q)$ contribute $O(q^{2n-3})$ to both moments. By Proposition~\ref{prop:low-moments}(ii) and~(iii), $\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}|\Sigma_n(h)|^2=q^{2n-1}+O(q^{2n-2})$ and $\sum_{h\in\mathbb{F}_q^n}\Sigma_n(h)^2=O(q^{2n-2})$. Dividing by $q^{2n-1}$ gives the two estimates. Now apply Lemma~\ref{lem:averages} with $T=S$ and $d=n$. For the first estimate take $\mathcal E=\mathcal W_n\otimes\mathcal W_n^\vee$, which is pure of weight $0$ with trace $|A^0_q(h)|^2$ at $h$ and with $\dim\big(V\otimes V^\vee\big)^G=\dim\operatorname{End}_G(V)$. For the second take $\mathcal E=\mathcal W_n^0\otimes\mathcal W_n^0$, where $\mathcal W_n^0=\mathcal W_n\otimes\gamma^{\deg}$ and $\gamma\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$ is the element with $\iota_{\mathbb C}(\gamma)=p^{-(n+1)/2}>0$; its trace at $h\in S(\mathbb{F}_q)$ is $A^0_q(h)^2$, and $G$ acts on its geometric generic stalk $V\otimes V$. Hence $\dim\operatorname{End}_G(V)=1$ and $(V\otimes V)^G=0$. As $V$ is semisimple, the first equality means that $V$ is irreducible. The second means $\operatorname{Hom}_G(V^\vee,V)=0$.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{prop:unipotent}
For every $n\ge2$ the group $G$ contains a unipotent element $g\ne1$ with $\operatorname{rank}(g-1)=r(n-1)$. In particular $G$ is infinite.
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Choose $c\in(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^\times)^{n-1}$. The inclusion $C_c\subset S$ induces a homomorphism $\pi_1(C_c\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)\to\pi_1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$. Through it, the inertia group at $h_1=0$ acts on $V$ by the local monodromy of $\mathcal W_n|_{C_c}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:boundary}(ii), a topological generator of tame inertia acts by a unipotent $g$ with $\operatorname{rank}(g-1)=r(n-1)\ge1$. In characteristic $0$ such an element has infinite order, since $g^m=\exp(m\log g)$ and $\log g\ne0$.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{prop:det}
For every $n\ge2$, the character $\det\mathcal W_n$ of $\pi_1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ has finite image $\Gamma$, and $\det(G)=\Gamma$. Consequently $G\cap\{\text{scalars}\}$ is finite.
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Let $\rho\colon\pi_1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be the representation defined by $\mathcal W_n$, so that $\Gamma$ is the image of $\det\circ\rho$.

\emph{Step 1: inertia.} By symmetry in the coordinates, Theorem~\ref{thm:boundary} applies to every coordinate line in every direction. Fix $i$ and a line $C\subset S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ along which the coordinates $h_j$, $j\ne i$, are constant. Through the homomorphism $\pi_1(C)\to\pi_1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$, the inertia group $I_0$ at $h_i=0$ acts on $V$ by the local monodromy of $\mathcal W_n|_C$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:boundary}(ii) the wild inertia acts trivially, so the action factors through the procyclic tame quotient of $I_0$, a topological generator of which acts by a unipotent element $g$. The image of $I_0$ therefore lies in the closure of the group generated by $g$, on which the continuous character $\det$ is identically $1$, because $\det g=1$. Thus $\det\circ\rho$ is trivial on $I_0$.

\emph{Step 2: characters of order prime to $p$.} Let $m\ge1$ be prime to $p$. As $S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ is connected, the continuous homomorphisms $\pi_1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)\to\mathbb Z/m$ are the elements of $H^1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mathbb Z/m)$, which we identify with $H^1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mu_m)$ by choosing a primitive $m$-th root of unity in $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$. The Kummer sequence $1\to\mu_m\to\mathbb{G}_m\xrightarrow{\,m\,}\mathbb{G}_m\to1$, exact for the \'etale topology because $p\nmid m$, gives an exact sequence
\[
0\to\mathcal O(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)^\times\big/\mathcal O(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)^{\times m}\to H^1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mu_m)\to\mathrm{Pic}(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)[m]\to0.
\]
The ring $\mathcal O(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)=\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p[h_1^{\pm1},\dots,h_n^{\pm1}]$ is factorial, so $\mathrm{Pic}(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)=0$ and the first map is an isomorphism. The units of this ring are $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^\times\cdot h_1^{\mathbb Z}\cdots h_n^{\mathbb Z}$, and $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^\times$ is $m$-divisible. Hence
\[
H^1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p,\mu_m)\cong(\mathbb Z/m)^n,
\]
with basis the Kummer classes of $h_1,\dots,h_n$. Let $\chi$ be the character attached to the class of $h_1^{e_1}\cdots h_n^{e_n}$, and let $C$ be as in Step~1. On $C$ the functions $h_j$, $j\ne i$, are constants, hence $m$-th powers in $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^\times$, so $\chi|_{\pi_1(C)}$ is the Kummer character of $h_i^{e_i}$. Its restriction to $I_0$ is the $e_i$-th power of the character $\sigma\mapsto\sigma(h_i^{1/m})/h_i^{1/m}$. This character maps $I_0$ onto $\mu_m$, because $h_i$ is a uniformizer at $0$, so that adjoining $h_i^{1/m}$ gives a totally ramified extension of degree $m$. Hence $\chi$ is trivial on $I_0$ if and only if $m\mid e_i$. Consequently a character of $\pi_1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ of finite order prime to $p$ that is trivial on the inertia groups of Step~1 for $i=1,\dots,n$ is trivial.

\emph{Step 3: $\Gamma$ is finite.} The group $\Gamma$ is compact, since $\pi_1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ is. The group $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell^\times$ is the union of the closed subgroups $E^\times$, where $E\subset\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$ runs over the countably many finite extensions of $\mathbb Q_\ell$. By the Baire category theorem some $\Gamma\cap E^\times$ has nonempty interior in $\Gamma$; it is then an open subgroup, of finite index. Enlarging $E$ by a finite set of coset representatives, we may assume $\Gamma\subseteq E^\times$. The valuation $v$ of $E$ maps $\Gamma$ onto a compact subgroup of the discrete torsion-free group $v(E^\times)$, which is finite and hence trivial; so $\Gamma\subseteq\mathcal O_E^\times$. Now $\mathcal O_E^\times$ is the product of a finite group and the pro-$\ell$ group $1+\mathfrak m_E$. The profinite abelian group $\Gamma$ is the product of its pro-$p$ part $\Gamma_p$ and its prime-to-$p$ part $\Gamma'$. Indeed, $\Gamma$ is the inverse limit of its finite quotients, each finite abelian group is canonically the product of its $p$-part and its prime-to-$p$ part, and these decompositions are compatible with the transition maps. As $\ell\ne p$, the group $\Gamma_p$ meets $1+\mathfrak m_E$ trivially, so it embeds into the finite group $\mathcal O_E^\times/(1+\mathfrak m_E)$ and is finite. If $\Gamma'\ne1$, then $\Gamma'$ has a nontrivial finite quotient, whose order is prime to $p$, and hence a nontrivial continuous character $\chi_0$ of finite order prime to $p$. Composing $\det\circ\rho$, which maps onto $\Gamma$, with the projection $\Gamma\to\Gamma'$ and with $\chi_0$ gives a nontrivial character of $\pi_1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ of order prime to $p$. By Step~1 it is trivial on all the inertia groups considered there, which contradicts Step~2. Hence $\Gamma'=1$, and $\Gamma=\Gamma_p$ is finite.

\emph{Step 4.} The subset $\det^{-1}(\Gamma)$ of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is Zariski closed and contains the image of $\rho$, so it contains $G$. Therefore $\det(G)=\Gamma$. If $z\cdot1\in G$, then $z^{r(n)}=\det(z\cdot1)\in\Gamma$, which leaves finitely many possibilities for $z$.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:larsen}
Let $V$ be a vector space of dimension $N\ge2$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic $0$, and let $H\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a Zariski-closed subgroup with $H^0$ reductive and $M_4(H,V)=2$. Then either $H^0\supseteq\operatorname{SL}(V)$, or $H^0$ consists of scalars. In the second case $H/(H\cap\{\text{scalars}\})$ is finite.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:semisimple}(i), every finite-dimensional representation of $H$ is semisimple. Let $H$ act on $\operatorname{End}(V)=V\otimes V^\vee$ by conjugation. A permutation of the tensor factors identifies $V^{\otimes2}\otimes(V^\vee)^{\otimes2}$ with $\operatorname{End}(V)\otimes\operatorname{End}(V)^\vee=\operatorname{End}_k(\operatorname{End}(V))$, compatibly with the action of $H$, so $\dim\operatorname{End}_H(\operatorname{End}(V))=M_4(H,V)=2$. Since $k$ has characteristic $0$, we have $N\ne0$ in $k$, and the trace gives a decomposition $\operatorname{End}(V)=k\cdot1\oplus\mathfrak{sl}(V)$ into $H$-stable subspaces. Accordingly,
\[
\operatorname{End}_H(\operatorname{End}(V))=\operatorname{End}_H(k\cdot1)\oplus\operatorname{Hom}_H(k\cdot1,\mathfrak{sl}(V))\oplus\operatorname{Hom}_H(\mathfrak{sl}(V),k\cdot1)\oplus\operatorname{End}_H(\mathfrak{sl}(V)).
\]
The first and the last summands contain the identity maps and are nonzero, as $\mathfrak{sl}(V)\ne0$. The total dimension is $2$, so both are one-dimensional and the two cross terms vanish. Thus the semisimple $H$-module $\mathfrak{sl}(V)$ has a one-dimensional endomorphism algebra, and it is irreducible.

Let $\mathfrak h\subseteq\operatorname{End}(V)$ be the Lie algebra of $H$. For $g\in H$, conjugation by $g$ preserves $H$, so its differential, which is conjugation by $g$ on $\operatorname{End}(V)$, preserves $\mathfrak h$. Thus $\mathfrak h\cap\mathfrak{sl}(V)$ is an $H$-stable subspace of $\mathfrak{sl}(V)$, equal to $0$ or to $\mathfrak{sl}(V)$. In characteristic $0$ every group scheme of finite type over $k$ is smooth, by Cartier's theorem. Hence the Lie algebra of the intersection of two closed subgroups of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is the intersection of their Lie algebras, and every algebraic group has the dimension of its Lie algebra.

If $\mathfrak h\cap\mathfrak{sl}(V)=\mathfrak{sl}(V)$, then $(H\cap\operatorname{SL}(V))^0$ is a closed connected subgroup of $\operatorname{SL}(V)$ of dimension $\dim\mathfrak{sl}(V)=\dim\operatorname{SL}(V)$. Since $\operatorname{SL}(V)$ is connected, hence irreducible as a variety, a closed irreducible subset of the same dimension is all of $\operatorname{SL}(V)$. Thus $(H\cap\operatorname{SL}(V))^0=\operatorname{SL}(V)$, and $\operatorname{SL}(V)\subseteq H^0$.

If $\mathfrak h\cap\mathfrak{sl}(V)=0$, then $\dim\mathfrak h\le1$. The projection $X\mapsto X-N^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(X)\cdot1$ of $\operatorname{End}(V)$ onto $\mathfrak{sl}(V)$ is $H$-equivariant, and it maps $\mathfrak h$ onto an $H$-stable subspace of $\mathfrak{sl}(V)$ of dimension at most $1<N^2-1$. This subspace is therefore $0$, that is, $\mathfrak h\subseteq k\cdot1$. Let $Z\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be the group of scalars. Then $H^0\cap Z$ has Lie algebra $\mathfrak h\cap k\cdot1=\mathfrak h$, hence the same dimension as the irreducible variety $H^0$, and $H^0=(H^0\cap Z)^0\subseteq Z$. Finally $H^0\subseteq H\cap Z$, so $H/(H\cap Z)$ is a quotient of the finite group $H/H^0$.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:monodromy}
For every $n\ge2$ and every odd prime $p$, $G^0=\operatorname{SL}_{r(n)}$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
\emph{Step 1: $G^0\subseteq\operatorname{SL}(V)$ and $\dim G^0\ge1$, for every $n\ge2$.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:det}, $\det(G^0)$ is a subgroup of the finite group $\det(G)$. It is connected, being the image of a connected group under a morphism of algebraic groups, and is therefore trivial. Thus $G^0\subseteq\operatorname{SL}(V)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:unipotent} the group $G$ is infinite; since it has finitely many connected components, $\dim G^0\ge1$.

\emph{Step 2: the case $n\ge3$.} By Corollary~\ref{cor:M4}, $M_4(G,V)=2$, and $G^0$ is reductive, being semisimple. So Theorem~\ref{thm:larsen} applies to $H=G$. The group $G^0$ does not consist of scalars, for it would then be contained in $G\cap\{\text{scalars}\}$, which is finite by Proposition~\ref{prop:det}, whereas $\dim G^0\ge1$. Hence $G^0\supseteq\operatorname{SL}(V)$, and therefore $G^0=\operatorname{SL}(V)$.

\emph{Step 3: the case $n=2$.} Here $\dim V=r(2)=2$, and the fourth moment gives no information: for $n=2$ the bounds of Propositions~\ref{prop:zero} and~\ref{prop:generic} are of the same order $q^{3n+2}$ as the main term of Proposition~\ref{prop:diag-main}. We argue directly instead. Let $\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathfrak{sl}_2$ be the Lie algebra of the connected reductive group $G^0$. In characteristic $0$ the Lie algebra of a connected reductive group is reductive, so $\mathfrak h=\mathfrak z(\mathfrak h)\oplus[\mathfrak h,\mathfrak h]$ with $[\mathfrak h,\mathfrak h]$ semisimple. If $[\mathfrak h,\mathfrak h]\ne0$, it is therefore a nonzero semisimple subalgebra of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, hence of dimension at least $3$. So $\mathfrak h=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, and $G^0=\operatorname{SL}_2$, because $\operatorname{SL}_2$ is connected of dimension $3$. If $[\mathfrak h,\mathfrak h]=0$, then $G^0$ is commutative, since in characteristic $0$ a connected algebraic group with abelian Lie algebra is commutative; being reductive, it is a torus, conjugate into the diagonal torus of $\operatorname{SL}_2$; it contains no unipotent element other than $1$. But for the element $g$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:unipotent} some power $g^m$ with $m\ge1$ lies in $G^0$, and $g^m=1+m(g-1)\ne1$, because $(g-1)^2=0$ in dimension two. Hence $G^0=\operatorname{SL}_2$.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:no-classification}
Larsen's alternative leaves two possibilities, $G^0\supseteq\operatorname{SL}(V)$ or $G$ finite modulo scalars, and the second is excluded by the unipotent element of Proposition~\ref{prop:unipotent}, which has infinite order. So no list of finite subgroups of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$, and in particular neither the classification of finite simple groups nor the results of Guralnick and Tiep on finite primitive groups, enters the proof. The same holds for the determination of the component group below, which uses only the local monodromy at infinity and Artin--Schreier theory.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:AS-lines}
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p$, let $S_k=\mathbb{G}_{m,k}^n$, and let $\chi\colon\pi_1(S_k)\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell^\times$ be a continuous character whose image is a finite $p$-group. Suppose that for every $i$ and every $c\in(k^\times)^{n-1}$ the restriction of $\chi$ to the fundamental group of the coordinate line $L_{i,c}=\{h:h_j=c_j\ \text{for}\ j\ne i\}$ is trivial. Then $\chi$ is trivial.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
The image of $\chi$ is cyclic of order $p^e$. We argue by induction on $e$, the case $e=0$ being trivial. The character $\chi^p$ satisfies the same hypothesis and has image of order $p^{e-1}$, so it is trivial by induction; hence $e\le1$. Suppose $e=1$. Choosing a primitive $p$-th root of unity in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$, we may regard $\chi$ as an element of $H^1(S_k,\mathbb F_p)=\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_1(S_k),\mathbb F_p)$. Let $A=k[h_1^{\pm1},\dots,h_n^{\pm1}]$ and $\wp(x)=x^p-x$. The Artin--Schreier sequence $0\to\mathbb F_p\to\mathcal O\xrightarrow{\wp}\mathcal O\to0$ on the \'etale site, together with $H^1(S_k,\mathcal O)=0$, identifies $H^1(S_k,\mathbb F_p)$ with $A/\wp(A)$, compatibly with restriction to the lines $L_{i,c}$, for which the same identification holds with $A$ replaced by $k[h_i^{\pm1}]$.

Let $\mathsf M=\mathbb Z^n\smallsetminus p\mathbb Z^n$. Every class in $A/\wp(A)$ is represented by a Laurent polynomial $g=\sum_{m\in\mathsf M}a_mh^m$: constants lie in $\wp(k)$ since $k$ is algebraically closed, and $a\,h^{pm}\equiv a^{1/p}h^m$ modulo $\wp(A)$. This representative is unique. Indeed, if $\sum_{m\in\mathsf M}a_mh^m=\wp(b)$ with $b=\sum_mb_mh^m$ nonconstant, choose $m_0\ne0$ in the support of $b$ with $\max_i|m_{0,i}|$ maximal; then $pm_0$ is not in the support of $b$, so the coefficient of $h^{pm_0}$ in $\wp(b)$ is $b_{m_0}^p\ne0$, although $pm_0\notin\mathsf M$. So $b$ is constant, and then all $a_m$ vanish. The same holds in one variable.

Let $g=\sum_{m\in\mathsf M}a_mh^m$ represent $\chi$, fix $i$, and for $c\in(k^\times)^{n-1}$ write $m=(m',m_i)$ and $c^{m'}=\prod_{j\ne i}c_j^{m_j}$. The restriction of $g$ to $L_{i,c}$ is $\sum_{e\in\mathbb Z}\alpha_e(c)h_i^e$ with $\alpha_e(c)=\sum_{m_i=e}a_mc^{m'}$. Its reduced representative in one variable has, for $e\notin p\mathbb Z$, the coefficient $\sum_{s\ge0}\alpha_{p^se}(c)^{1/p^s}$ of $h_i^e$. By hypothesis these coefficients vanish for all $c$. Raising to a large power $p^N$, we find that the Laurent polynomial $\sum_{s\ge0}\sum_{m_i=p^se}a_m^{p^{N-s}}c^{p^{N-s}m'}$ vanishes on $(k^\times)^{n-1}$, hence identically. Distinct pairs $(s,m)$ give distinct monomials $c^{p^{N-s}m'}$. Indeed, for fixed $s$ the exponent $m$ is determined by $m'$, as $m_i=p^se$. And if $p^{N-s}m'=p^{N-\tilde s}\tilde m'$ with $s<\tilde s$, then $\tilde m=p^{\tilde s-s}m\in p\mathbb Z^n$, which is impossible. So $a_m=0$ whenever $m_i\ne0$. As every $m\in\mathsf M$ has a nonzero coordinate, $g=0$, and $\chi$ is trivial.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:det}
For every $n\ge2$ there is $\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell^\times$ with $\det\mathcal W_n\cong\mathcal{L}_\psi(-2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}(h_1+\cdots+h_n))\otimes\alpha^{\deg}$, where $\alpha^{\deg}$ is the geometrically constant sheaf of rank one on which $\operatorname{Frob}_p$ acts by $\alpha$. The image $\Gamma$ of $\det\mathcal W_n$ on $\pi_1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ is the group $\mu_p$ of $p$-th roots of unity.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Put $\mathcal D=\det\mathcal W_n\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}(h_1+\cdots+h_n))$, and let $\chi$ be the character of $\pi_1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ that it defines. By Proposition~\ref{prop:det} and its proof, the image of $\det\mathcal W_n$ on $\pi_1(S\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ is a finite $p$-group, and the image of the Artin--Schreier sheaf lies in $\mu_p$; so the image of $\chi$ is a finite $p$-group. The family is symmetric in the coordinates, so Theorem~\ref{thm:infinity}(ii) applies to the coordinate lines $L_{i,c}$ in every direction $i$. On $L_{i,c}$ the sheaf $\mathcal{L}_\psi(2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}(h_1+\cdots+h_n))$ is $\mathcal{L}_\psi(2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}h_i)$ tensored with a geometrically constant sheaf, so $\chi$ is trivial on $\pi_1(L_{i,c})$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:AS-lines}, $\chi$ is trivial, that is, $\mathcal D$ is geometrically constant. A lisse sheaf of rank one on $S$ that is geometrically constant is of the form $\alpha^{\deg}$, which proves the first assertion. Finally $2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}\ne0$ in $\mathbb{F}_p$, as $p$ is odd. So the restriction of $\mathcal{L}_\psi(-2^{n-1}\lambda^{-1}(h_1+\cdots+h_n))$ to a coordinate line is a nontrivial Artin--Schreier sheaf, of Swan conductor $1$ at $\infty$; its geometric image is a nontrivial subgroup of $\mu_p$, hence equal to $\mu_p$.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:Ggeom}
For every $n\ge2$ and every odd prime $p$,
\[
G_{\mathrm{geom}}(\mathcal W_n)=\big\{g\in\operatorname{GL}(V):\det(g)^p=1\big\}.
\]
In particular Theorem~\ref{thmE}(ii) holds.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:monodromy}, $G^0=\operatorname{SL}(V)$, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:det} and Theorem~\ref{thm:det}, $\det(G)=\Gamma=\mu_p$. So $G\subseteq\{g:\det(g)\in\mu_p\}$. Conversely, let $\det(g)\in\mu_p$. Choose $g'\in G$ with $\det g'=\det g$. Then $g'^{-1}g\in\operatorname{SL}(V)=G^0\subseteq G$, so $g\in G$. The component group $G/G^0=G/\operatorname{SL}(V)$ is isomorphic to $\mu_p$ through $\det$.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:n2-consistency}
For $n=2$, Corollary~\ref{cor:M2} shows independently that $\det$ is nontrivial on $G$. Indeed, if $\det$ were trivial on $G$, then $G=\operatorname{SL}_2$, and the standard representation of $\operatorname{SL}_2$ is self-dual, contradicting $(V\otimes V)^G=0$. For $n\ge3$ the non-self-duality in Corollary~\ref{cor:M2} carries no information on the determinant, since the standard representation of $\operatorname{SL}_r$ is not self-dual for $r\ge3$.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:numerology}
Let $n\ge1$.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $2S_1(n)=(n+1)b_n-2^n$.
\item $e(1)=0$, and $e(n)=2e(n-1)+2^{n-1}-1$ if $n\ge2$.
\item $2^n-1+e(n)-S_1(n)=\frac12(n+1)r(n)$ and $e(n)-\sum_{k\ge1}(k-1)m_{n,k}=\frac12(n-1)r(n)$. In particular $(n+1)r(n)$ and $(n-1)r(n)$ are even.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
(i) Put $K=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Since $m_{n,k}=\binom nk-\binom n{k-1}$, summation by parts gives
\[
S_1(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{K}k\binom nk-\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}(j+1)\binom nj=K\binom nK-\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\binom nj .
\]
If $n=2K$, the symmetry $\binom nj=\binom n{n-j}$ gives $\sum_{j<K}\binom nj=\frac12(2^n-b_n)$, so $2S_1(n)=2Kb_n-2^n+b_n$. If $n=2K+1$, it gives $\sum_{j\le K}\binom nj=2^{n-1}$, so $\sum_{j<K}\binom nj=2^{n-1}-b_n$ and $2S_1(n)=2Kb_n-2^n+2b_n$. In both cases $2S_1(n)=(n+1)b_n-2^n$.

(ii) $2e(n-1)+2^{n-1}-1=(n-3)2^{n-1}+2+2^{n-1}-1=e(n)$.

(iii) By (i), $2\big(2^n-1+e(n)-S_1(n)\big)=2^{n+1}+(n-2)2^n+2^n-(n+1)b_n=(n+1)r(n)$. Since $\sum_{k\ge0}m_{n,k}=b_n$ and $m_{n,0}=1$, we have $\sum_{k\ge1}(k-1)m_{n,k}=S_1(n)-b_n+1$, and therefore $e(n)-\sum_{k\ge1}(k-1)m_{n,k}=\big(2^n-1+e(n)-S_1(n)\big)-(2^n-b_n)=\frac12(n+1)r(n)-r(n)$. The left-hand sides of both identities are integers.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:FT-zero}
Put $P=j_{v!}\mathcal R[n-1]$, a complex on $\mathbb A^1_v$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $H^i_c(U\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f'))=0$ for $i\ne n-1$, and there is an exact sequence of $\operatorname{Frob}_q$-modules
\[
0\to H^{n-2}_c(Y_c\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f'))\to H^{n-1}_c(U\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f'))\to\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell\to0,
\]
with $\operatorname{Frob}_q$ acting trivially on $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$. In particular $H^{n-1}_c(U\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f'))$ has dimension $2^{n-1}$, and the determinant of $\operatorname{Frob}_q$ on it is $D_{n-1}(c)$.
\item $P$ is a perverse sheaf, and $P|_{U_v}\cong F[1]$.
\item $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P)\cong\mathcal G[1]$ for a constructible sheaf $\mathcal G$ on $\mathbb A^1_{h_1}$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ that has no nonzero section supported on a finite set. Moreover $\mathcal G|_{\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}}\cong\mathcal G_n|_{C_c}(1)$, and $\mathcal G_0\cong H^{n-1}_c(U\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f'))$ compatibly with $\operatorname{Frob}_q$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
(i) The phase is $f'$ on $\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}$, on its open subset $U$ and on the closed complement $Y_c$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:t0} for $n-1$ variables, $R\Gamma_c(\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f'))$ is a line placed in degree $n-1$, with trivial Frobenius. If $n\ge3$, Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}(iv), applied to $n-1\ge2$ variables and to $c$, shows that $R\Gamma_c(Y_c\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f'))$ is concentrated in degree $n-2$, of dimension $2^{n-1}-1$; if $n=2$, this holds because $Y_c$ is a point. The excision sequence for $Y_c\subset\mathbb{G}_m^{n-1}$ gives the assertions.

(ii) By Lemma~\ref{lem:R-global}, $P|_{U_v}\cong F[1]$. Let $P_i={}^p\mathcal H^i(j_{v!}\mathcal R)$ be the perverse cohomology sheaves. The functor $\operatorname{FT}_\psi$ is triangulated and maps perverse sheaves to perverse sheaves \cite[Th.~(1.3.2.3)]{Laumon}; as the perverse t-structure is bounded, every object is a successive extension of shifted perverse sheaves, so $\operatorname{FT}_\psi$ is t-exact, and $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P_i)\cong{}^p\mathcal H^i\big(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(j_{v!}\mathcal R)\big)$. By~\eqref{eq:FT-model}, $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(j_{v!}\mathcal R)|_{\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}}\cong\big(\mathcal G_n|_{C_c}(1)[1]\big)[-(n-1)]$, and $\mathcal G_n|_{C_c}(1)[1]$ is perverse by (P1). Restriction to an open subset is t-exact, so $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P_i)$ vanishes on $\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}$ for $i\ne n-1$. Now let $\mathcal Q$ be a perverse sheaf on $\mathbb A^1_{h_1}$ that vanishes on $\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}$. By (P2), $\mathcal H^{-1}(\mathcal Q)$ is a sheaf supported at $0$ without nonzero sections supported at $0$, so it vanishes, and $\mathcal Q=i_{0*}E$, where $E$ is a finite-dimensional continuous representation of $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q/\mathbb{F}_q)$ placed in degree $0$. For such an $E$, let $\bar E$ be the geometrically constant sheaf on $\mathbb A^1_v$ with fibre $E$; Lemma~\ref{lem:integrate-t} and the projection formula give $\operatorname{FT}_\psi\big(\bar E(1)[1]\big)\cong i_{0*}E$. Since $\operatorname{FT}_\psi$ is an equivalence of categories \cite[Cor.~(1.2.2.3)]{Laumon}, it follows that $P_i\cong\bar E_i(1)[1]$ for $i\ne n-1$, where $E_i=i_0^*\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P_i)$. On the other hand $P_i|_{U_v}={}^p\mathcal H^i\big(F[1][-(n-1)]\big)=0$ for $i\ne n-1$, and a lisse sheaf on $\mathbb A^1_v$ that vanishes on $U_v$ is zero. Hence $P_i=0$ for $i\ne n-1$. Therefore $j_{v!}\mathcal R\cong P_{n-1}[-(n-1)]$, and $P\cong P_{n-1}$ is perverse.

(iii) By (ii) and \cite[Th.~(1.3.2.3)]{Laumon}, $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P)$ is perverse, and by~\eqref{eq:FT-model} its restriction to $\mathbb{G}_{m,h_1}$ is $\mathcal G_n|_{C_c}(1)[1]$. By proper base change, its stalk at $h_1=0$ is
\[
R\Gamma_c(\mathbb A^1_v\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,P)[1]=R\Gamma_c(\mathbb{G}_{m,v}\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal R)[n]=R\Gamma_c(U\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f'))[n],
\]
compatibly with $\operatorname{Frob}_q$, and by (i) this is $H^{n-1}_c(U\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f'))$ placed in degree $-1$. Hence $\mathcal H^0(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P))=0$, and (P2) gives the assertions, with $\mathcal G=\mathcal H^{-1}(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P))$.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:vanishing-zero}
Let $D_0$ be a decomposition group at the rational point $h_1=0$ of $\mathbb A^1_{h_1}$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, let $I_0\subseteq D_0$ be its inertia subgroup, and let $\phi\in D_0$ induce the geometric Frobenius of $\mathbb{F}_q$. Let $\mathcal G$ be the sheaf of Lemma~\ref{lem:FT-zero}(iii), and let $\mathcal G_{\bar\eta_0}$ be its generic stalk, a representation of $D_0$. Then there is an exact sequence of representations of $D_0$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:vanishing-zero}
0\longrightarrow\mathcal G_0\longrightarrow\mathcal G_{\bar\eta_0}\longrightarrow\bar F_\infty(-1)\longrightarrow0,
\end{equation}
in which $D_0$ acts on $\mathcal G_0$ and on $\bar F_\infty(-1)$ through $D_0/I_0=\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q/\mathbb{F}_q)$. Moreover $\bar F_\infty\cong H^{n-2}_c(Y_c\otimes\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q,\mathcal{L}_\psi(f'))$ as $\operatorname{Frob}_q$-modules, and
\[
\det\big(\phi\mid\mathcal G_{\bar\eta_0}\big)=q^{2^{n-1}-1}D_{n-1}(c)^2 .
\]
In particular $I_0$ acts unipotently on $\mathcal G_{\bar\eta_0}$, and this determinant does not depend on the choice of $\phi$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Let $T_0$ be the henselization of $\mathbb A^1_{h_1}$ at $0$, let $\eta$ be its generic point and $\bar\eta$ a geometric point over $\eta$, so that $D_0=\mathrm{Gal}(\bar\eta/\eta)$. For a scheme $\mathcal X$ of finite type over $T_0$ and a complex $\mathcal Q$ on $\mathcal X$, we use the complexes of nearby cycles $R\Psi(\mathcal Q)$ and of vanishing cycles $R\Phi(\mathcal Q)$ on the geometric special fibre $\mathcal X_{\bar0}$, with their compatible actions of $D_0$, and the distinguished triangle $\mathcal Q|_{\mathcal X_{\bar0}}\to R\Psi(\mathcal Q)\to R\Phi(\mathcal Q)\to$ \cite[Exp.~XIII, 2.1]{SGA7}. For a complex $\mathcal Q$ on $\mathbb A^1_{h_1}$ we write $R\Phi_0(\mathcal Q)$ for $R\Phi(\mathcal Q|_{T_0})$, a complex of representations of $D_0$.

\emph{The exact sequence.} For $\mathcal Q=\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P)=\mathcal G[1]$, the first two terms of the triangle are $\mathcal G_0[1]$ and $\mathcal G_{\bar\eta_0}[1]$, and the first map is the specialization map $\mathcal G_0\to\mathcal G_{\bar\eta_0}$. This map is injective, because its kernel is the stalk at $0$ of the subsheaf of sections of $\mathcal G$ supported at $0$, which vanishes by Lemma~\ref{lem:FT-zero}(iii). Hence $R\Phi_0(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P))$ is concentrated in degree $-1$, and there is an exact sequence of representations of $D_0$
\[
0\to\mathcal G_0\to\mathcal G_{\bar\eta_0}\to R^{-1}\Phi_0\big(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P)\big)\to0 .
\]
It remains to show that $R^{-1}\Phi_0(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(P))\cong\bar F_\infty(-1)$.

\emph{Localization at $v=\infty$.} Let $\bar X=\mathbb P^1_v\times\mathbb A^1_{h_1}$, let $\iota_X\colon\mathbb A^1_v\times\mathbb A^1_{h_1}\hookrightarrow\bar X$ be the inclusion, and let $\bar p\colon\bar X\to\mathbb A^1_{h_1}$ be the projection, which is proper. For a complex $K$ on $\mathbb A^1_v$ put $\mathcal J(K)=\iota_{X!}\big(\operatorname{pr}_v^*K\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(vh_1)\big)$, so that $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K)=R\bar p_*\mathcal J(K)[1]$. Nearby cycles commute with proper direct images \cite[Exp.~XIII, (2.1.7.2)]{SGA7}, and so does restriction to the special fibre, by proper base change; hence so do vanishing cycles, and
\[
R\Phi_0\big(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K)\big)\cong R\Gamma\big(\mathbb P^1_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q},R\Phi(\mathcal J(K))\big)[1]
\]
compatibly with the actions of $D_0$, where $R\Phi(\mathcal J(K))$ is formed for $\bar X\times_{\mathbb A^1_{h_1}}T_0$ over $T_0$. By Deligne's theorem \cite[Th.~finitude, Cor.~2.16]{SGA45}, the structure morphism $\mathbb A^1_v\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{F}_q$ is universally locally acyclic relative to $K$; the theorem is stated there for torsion coefficients, and the case of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell$-complexes follows by passage to the limit and d\'evissage. By base change, the projection $\mathbb A^1_v\times T_0\to T_0$ is locally acyclic relative to $\operatorname{pr}_v^*K$, and hence also relative to $\operatorname{pr}_v^*K\otimes\mathcal{L}_\psi(vh_1)$, as $\mathcal{L}_\psi(vh_1)$ is lisse. So $R\Phi(\mathcal J(K))$ vanishes on $\mathbb A^1_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q}$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:localization}
R\Phi_0\big(\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K)\big)\cong R\Phi\big(\mathcal J(K)\big)_{\infty}[1],
\end{equation}
where the right-hand side is the stalk at the point $v=\infty$ of the geometric special fibre. This is the localization step in Laumon's computation of the local monodromy of $\operatorname{FT}_\psi(K)$ at a finite point of the dual line \cite[Prop.~(2.3.2.1)(i)]{Laumon}.

\emph{Comparison with the constant sheaf.} Let $N_\infty=\mathbb P^1_v\smallsetminus\{0,s\}$, an open neighbourhood of $\infty$ on which $\bar F$ is lisse, and let $K_0=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell[1]$ be the constant sheaf on $\mathbb A^1_v$ placed in degree $-1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:FT-zero}(ii), $P=F[1]$ on $N_\infty\cap\mathbb A^1_v$, so the projection formula for $\iota_{X!}$ gives $\mathcal J(P)|_{N_\infty\times\mathbb A^1_{h_1}}\cong\operatorname{pr}_v^*\bar F\otimes\mathcal J(K_0)|_{N_\infty\times\mathbb A^1_{h_1}}$. Vanishing cycles are local for the \'etale topology, and they commute with tensor products by lisse sheaves: nearby cycles are computed by a direct image from the geometric generic fibre followed by restriction to the special fibre, and both operations commute with tensor products by lisse sheaves, by the projection formula, which is a local statement. Hence
\[
R\Phi\big(\mathcal J(P)\big)_\infty\cong\bar F_\infty\otimes R\Phi\big(\mathcal J(K_0)\big)_\infty,
\]
